item.content:encoded:
Heading into the Wild Card Series, one could make a case that the Red Sox had a chance to beat the Yankees. It would take two or three great starts from Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and/or Ranger Suarez, it would take some timely hitting to put two or three runs on the board per game, and it would take some lockdown relief innings from the back end of the bullpen.
Yet the Red Sox only got decent starts from Tolle and Gray, they set a new franchise record for offensive utility, and their bullpen was a catastrophe.
And the cherry on top was that their manager, who inked a contract extension last week, showed he certainly does not know how to manage in the postseason.
Other than that, did you enjoy the series?
Here's everything we learned from the ever-so-brief two-game sweep in the Wild Card Series, as the 2026 team technically failed to get as far as the 2025 Red Sox.
Red Sox set ugly new franchise record
Red Sox history spans 126 seasons, so it was a bit surprising to see the broadcast note early in Game 2 that Boston was in the midst of rewriting franchise history with the longest scoring drought to start a postseason ever.
Obviously, the Red Sox' offense has been stagnant (or worse) for weeks, but 26 previous trips to the playoffs, you'd figure that they had started off with a scoreless game and a half before.
Alas, nope. This drought was historic. It ended at 14.2 innings, broken by Willson Contreras' solo shot with two outs in the sixth inning.
And while some of it may be explained by the absences of Roman Anthony and Mickey Gasper, there's no excuse for a playoff team to be this helpless at the plate.
Chad Tracy is not a big-game manager right now
There may have been a case for Chad Tracy to pull Payton Tolle for Erik Miller in Game 1. Not really, but there could have been a case made for Miller's sinker being more effective against Ben Rice than Tolle's fastball.
Yet there's simply no way to understand why one night later, Tracy made the exact same move.
With Sonny Gray at just 70 pitches and the Yankees leading 1-0 with two outs in the fifth inning, Tracy went back to Miller, this time with two runners on base and Cody Bellinger at the plate. The left-left matchup was presumably the reason for the call, but Bellinger crushes sliders from lefties. And when Miller threw a slider to Bellinger ... he delivered.
Bellinger singled home a run, and Miller then gave up another hit to Luis Garcia Jr. The Red Sox only got out of the inning because Rice was caught at home after an aggressive send on that second single.
Gray's pitch count of 70 was tied for his second-lowest of the season, and though he had allowed two singles in the fifth, his body of work over the season and over the past 13 years gave him a much better chance of escaping the mini jam than Miller, who had a 2.045 WHIP and 7.36 ERA in the month of September and who gave up a home run and a single while getting just one out the night before.
If Tracy was insistent that Gray had to come out of the game, he had, quite literally, every high-leverage arm available to him. Instead, he went with Erik Miller.
And with that same complement of arms available in the bottom of the sixth inning, Tracy went with Garrett Crochet, who hasn't pitched in a game since April 25. It didn't go well.
Tracy also showed a lack of feel for the moment when he let leadoff hitter Jahmai Jones, who batted .129 with a .432 OPS over the final 13 games of the regular season and who struck out looking twice, to take his third at-bat in the sixth inning, with the Red Sox trailing 2-0.
Given Boston's offensive ineptitude, the bullpen decisions are perhaps all moot. But had this been a close series, or if the Red Sox find themselves in one in the future, Tracy will carry some major doubt regarding his ability to manage those games.
Simply put, Chad Tracy did not do a single thing right in these two high-stakes games.
More Red Sox Coverage
Luis Garcia Jr.'s home run was great hitting, not bad pitching
It took until the fourth inning for the Yankees to get to Sonny Gray, but the solo homer he allowed to Luis Garcia Jr. didn't come on a bad pitch at all.
Leading off the fourth, Garcia was behind in the count 1-2 when Gray tried to bury a sweeper down and in to the lefty. Gray hit his spot with a pitch that was set to hit the bottom of the strike zone. But Garcia simply stayed on the pitch and went down and got it.
Luis Gar-SEE-YA 🦁 pic.twitter.com/GqxScAqskG
— New York Yankees (@Yankees) October 1, 2026
With the Red Sox starved for runs, Garcia's solo shot was a jarring reminder that all it takes is one good swing to put a run on the board.
Boston eventually got that swing from Contreras in the sixth, but that jolt of hope for the visiting team didn't last long.
What could have been with Garrett Crochet ...
If you just looked at the box score, you'd be shocked to see Garrett Crochet's line. He faced four batters, allowing all of them to score. He didn't record an out, despite getting Spencer Jones to chase strike three to start the sixth inning.
Of course, some of that outcome was fair, as Crochet allowed back-to-back singles. But Caleb Durbin couldn't get the out at first on what was intended to be a sacrifice bunt, Crochet left with the bases loaded, and Garrett Whitlock -- who had a dreadful night -- couldn't limit the damage at all.
Such an outcome was perhaps expected, considering Crochet has not pitched in a game since April 25 due to shoulder problems. But you also can't help but wonder what would have happened if Adley Rutschman and Willson Contreras hadn't combined to bungle Crochet's inning-opening strikeout of Jones.
Rutschman took an extra beat to pounce on the ball that had bounced off his chest, and then he took an extra step before firing to first base. There, Contreras was planted on the back side of the base instead of the front. As a result, Jones was able to beat the throw.
Credit to Aaron Boone for challenging that call, which was initially an out on the field, but really, it wasn't even close.
Rutschman then compounded the matter by sailing a throw into center field when Jones stole second, allowing the runner to take third before scoring on a single. Had Rutschman made either of those two throws, it's fair to wonder how differently Crochet's inning could have gone.
Summing up the season
There will be plenty of time in the coming months to eulogize this season, but really, despite the 32-5 stretch in the summer, it wasn't one to celebrate.
Last year's team won a game in the Wild Card Series, a disappointing ending. This year's team couldn't even do that.
Injuries to Crochet and Anthony were certainly impactful, but this roster -- and particularly the offense -- was not built to contend for a World Series. The Red Sox scored two or fewer runs in 13 of their final 23 games, averaging 2.5 runs per game over that stretch.
With the season on the line, the Red Sox had Jahmai Jones, Nate Eaton and Nick Sogard in their starting lineup.
After trading three of their top-five prospects to acquire Adley Rutschman, the catcher batted .222 with a .688 OPS in the regular season before going 1-for-8 in the playoffs.
Willson Contreras, a 34-year-old former catcher with a lot of MLB miles on him, was worn down by the end of the season. Caleb Durbin, whose lows outnumbered his highs this year, went 0-for-7 in the playoffs. Ceddanne Rafaela posted the same numbers, too.
The return for Marcelo Mayer was Erik Miller, who made a strong first impression but played a pivotal role in sinking the team's chances in both postseason losses after an extremely unreliable final month of the season.
The starting pitching staff was excellent, and the bullpen was elite. But the overall roster construction will lead to plenty of questions about Craig Breslow's ability to build a real winner. Likewise, the two playoff games cast some serious doubt on whether Chad Tracy is a manager capable of winning games in October.
The 15-game winning streak and 32-5 stretch might have led to some internal victory laps and the decisions to stick with Breslow and Tracy for the foreseeable future. But the 2026 Red Sox, on the whole, were what they were: mediocre. And having been stuck in mediocrity (or worse) for half a decade, there won't be much more patience in and around Boston for it to continue.
Technically, the historic season turnaround may have been a positive, as making the playoffs beats bottoming out more often than not. But considering that the Red Sox likely could have loaded up on promising players by selling off veteran pieces like Contreras, Gray, Aroldis Chapman and anyone else at the deadline, that run in July may have hurt the Red Sox in the long term -- especially with the prospect haul that went out to acquire Rutschman.
In any event, the Red Sox finished as the third-best team in the AL East, and they failed to win a single playoff game, getting outscored 18-2 in their lone playoff series. That's the final word on the season as the long offseason -- potentially longer than most -- awaits.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Sonny Gray's premature exit curses Chad Tracy, Red Sox into brutal Wild Card ending

item.content:encoded:
Boston Red Sox fans didn't want to see Chad Tracy emerge from the dugout in the bottom of the fifth inning. He should've learned from his Game 1 mistake.
But in Wild Card Game 2, Tracy pulled Sonny Gray after 4.2 frames to swap him for Erik Miller, just as he did with Payton Tolle the day before. Gray was having a better night than Tolle, though — he collected five strikeouts and allowed two runs on six hits. He was living on the edges and racked up swing-and-miss through 70 pitches.
Miller entered the game and immediately let up a single to Cody Bellinger. The Yankees took a 2-0 lead. The run was charged to Gray, but it didn't have to be that way. Miller posted a brutal September and struggled similarly in his first Wild Card outing. The choice to turn to him again, especially with the season on the line, is inexplicable.
Tracy's bullpen management didn't get any better. Garrett Crochet entered the game in the sixth inning and immediately got unlucky. Spencer Jones struck out swinging at a pitch in the dirt and Adley Rutschman couldn't get a good block on it, which allowed Jones to take first base. Crochet pitched decently well, avoiding the middle of the plate, but he couldn't collect an out before New York plated another run and loaded the bases.
Chad Tracy pulling Sonny Gray early led to the Red Sox's downfall in Wild Card Game 2, as it did in Game 1 with Payton Tolle
Going to Crochet while the game was still within reach was another strange choice by Tracy. Crochet hadn't pitched in the big leagues since April 25 due to two different shoulder injuries — the Red Sox had no idea how he would fare in a game, but went to him anyway despite having Jake Bennett available.
Tracy's bullpen management choices certainly didn't make the Red Sox any better this series, but their offense deserves some blame for the way the Wild Card series went. Willson Contreras and Nick Sogard contributed solo home runs to prevent another shutout, but no one else gave them any help. Four hits, seven strikeouts and 0-for-2 with runners in scoring position won't cut it against any playoff team, let alone the Yankees' utterly dominant pitching staff.
Even so, Boston got more offense in the win-or-go-home game than it did in Game 1, and bad bullpen management did the Red Sox in again. Had Tracy kept Gray in the game, the score could've stayed closer and the game might've actually been winnable. Instead, an incredible, memorable season came to an end without ever reaching October, and the Red Sox did it to themselves.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox ace Sonny Gray frustrated by lack of trust from manager during Yankees rout

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — With the Boston bats ice cold at Yankee Stadium again, a couple of quick hooks by Red Sox rookie manager Chad Tracy led to another early postseason exit.
And top starter Sonny Gray wasn't happy about being lifted after only 70 pitches.
"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. I think that's a fact," Gray said. "I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment."
For the second consecutive season, the Red Sox were sent home for the winter by their biggest rivals as the New York Yankees rolled to a 9-2 victory Wednesday night and a two-game sweep of their Wild Card Series.
Boston was outscored 18-2 overall and left to lament a miserable finish to this roller-coaster ride of a season that included Tracy taking over when Alex Cora was fired in April.
Tracy's decision-making came under scrutiny after both playoff games against the Yankees. In Boston's 9-0 defeat a night earlier, Tracy pulled rookie starter Payton Tolle after 4 2/3 innings and 83 pitches in a 1-0 game.
Last year, the Red Sox won their Wild Card Series opener before losing to New York in a deciding Game 3 as they got overpowered by Cam Schlittler, who pitched another playoff gem against his hometown team Tuesday night.
"To have it end here two times in a row is tough," shortstop Trevor Story said.
Facing a Yankees lineup missing injured slugger Aaron Judge, the Red Sox gave up 26 hits in two games despite a pair of effective performances from their starting pitchers.
At the plate, Boston mustered only seven hits and finally snapped a 26-inning postseason scoring drought that dated to last year when Willson Contreras homered just over the right-center fence in the sixth Wednesday.
"It's obviously been an eventful year," Tracy said. "In the moment right now you can't think much more other than anything but the fact that we just lost a playoff series."
Needing a victory to extend their season, the Red Sox sent Gray to the mound and the 18-game winner certainly gave them a chance. Boston trailed 1-0 in the fifth when the right-hander allowed a two-out single to Ben Rice that put runners at the corners.
Tracy then yanked Gray, eager to hand the ball to baseball's best bullpen during the regular season.
"I felt good. You know, I felt crisp. I felt sharp. I felt like I was just out there competing. And yeah, I mean, I got clipped for a solo homer and then some singles, but I felt like I stayed on the attack throughout. I was just executing what I wanted to do," Gray said. "I'm frustrated, for sure. You know, not ready for it to end. A lot of emotions."
Asked about the move, Contreras put his finger over his lips to zip them shut.
"It's not enough when you have talent or you have data or you have computers that's telling you what to do, because this is baseball," he said. "The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day you are going to have to need experience and veteran guys to win games."
In both games of the series, Tracy gave the ball to left-handed reliever Erik Miller after taking out his starting pitcher.
On Tuesday, Rice greeted Miller with a 423-foot solo homer to straightaway center field.
On Wednesday, Tracy summoned Miller to face a different left-handed hitter, Cody Bellinger — who batted .274 against lefties this season and .259 versus right-handers. In fact, his .310 batting average against left-handers over the past two years was the best of any left-handed hitter in the majors.
Bellinger made Tracy and the Red Sox pay, lining an RBI single to right field.
"We're struggling to score runs," Tracy said. "And when you get in spots where you're struggling to score runs and you're already trailing, you feel like you've got to be aggressive and go."
Back from a shoulder injury, ace starter Garrett Crochet entered in the sixth for his first outing since April 25 and first relief appearance since 2023 with the Chicago White Sox. The left-hander opened with a strikeout, but Spencer Jones reached safely on a wild pitch, and Crochet never got an out.
Bellinger's three-run homer off right-hander Garrett Whitlock capped a six-run inning that made it 8-1, and the Red Sox were done. A bullpen that led the majors with a 3.00 ERA during the regular season finished this series with a 20.25 ERA after giving up 15 runs, 15 hits and seven walks in 6 2/3 innings, with a .484 opponents' batting average.
Boston's latest downfall in the Bronx was a crushing end to a wild 2026 season for the Red Sox, who stumbled to a 32-46 start. Tracy was the skipper at Triple-A Worcester before getting promoted to interim manager in Boston, and the team finally began to take off with a four-game sweep of the Yankees at Fenway Park in late June.
After clinching a wild-card spot last week, the Red Sox removed the interim tag and named Tracy the 49th manager in team history, signing him to a three-year contract that runs through the 2029 season, with a club option for 2030. The team also exercised the 2029 and 2030 options on chief baseball officer Craig Breslow.
"I wasn't there for the highs and lows," Crochet said. "For this team to do what it did do, to make it to this point, was nothing short of miraculous."
Led by Gray and Contreras, among others, the Red Sox went on a 15-game winning streak in July that equaled a franchise record and used a 32-5 surge to climb back into contention. They became the fourth team in major league history to reach the postseason after falling 14 games under .500, and the first to qualify after losing as many as 44 of its first 75.
Gray, who can become a free agent after the World Series, went around the clubhouse to hug each of his teammates following Wednesday's defeat.
"I'm proud of what we accomplished," the pitcher said. "We were left for dead there for a while."
___

item.title: [wcvb.com] Red Sox supporters keep faith before must-win Game 2
item.dc:creator: Peter Eliopoulos
item.description: Red Sox supporters keep faith before must-win Game 2 Red Sox fans are holding onto hope as the team prepares for the critical Game 2 of the AL Wild Card series against the New York Yankees after a disappointing loss that saw Boston give up nine unanswered runs. item.content:encoded:
Red Sox supporters keep faith before must-win Game 2
Red Sox fans are holding onto hope as the team prepares for the critical Game 2 of the AL Wild Card series against the New York Yankees after a disappointing loss that saw Boston give up nine unanswered runs.
In Boston’s Financial District on Wednesday, many fans were seen sporting Red Sox hats and gear while out for lunch.
“Everyone is nervous in the city right now, after watching last night, we just feel like hope is just dwindling away, but this whole season is what it’s all been about, so hoping for another one of those comebacks,” Ryan Palmer said.
While frustration over the team’s inability to score runs or get hits was evident, fans also acknowledged the strong performance by New York Yankees pitcher Cam Schlittler and praised Payton Tolle, though some felt he was pulled from the game too early.
“And with Tolle as pitcher, I think he really encapsulates the Red Sox spirit, the Boston spirit, so if they won it would be fun,” Elise Coakley said.
“Tolle looked good, tough pull,” Dan O'Donovan said.
Adding to the disappointment, Roman Anthony left the game early and will not play on Wednesday.
“It’s tough because he’s truly their one impact bat, or at least can be, and when he went down that was pretty deflating, and for them to just pile on the way they did was tough,” Patrick Curran said.
During the lunchtime rush at Paisani Food Truck downtown, fans were discussing the Red Sox while repping their favorite team.
“I think they could do it tonight, and then you paid Ranger Suárez all this money for game 3, so I think they can do it,” Curran said.
“Red Sox-Yankees, that’s a good rivalry, you’ve got to have it,” Marion Kennedy said.
“I’m a die-hard Sox fan, but I don’t see it, I don’t see it. They still gave us a good year,” another fan said.
“But I hope tonight we turn things around and we come back,” Doug Cavanaugh said.
“You just feel like they always have a chance, which is not how you felt earlier in the year, so you’ve got to be excited about it,” O'Donovan said.
Fans believe that if the Red Sox can secure a win in Game 2. It could set the stage for a decisive Game 3. However, a loss would likely mean the end of their season, leaving them to pack up and prepare for the offseason.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] AL Wild Card Series Game 2: Max Fried vs. Sonny Gray
item.dc:creator: Jeremy Nielsen
item.description: In the words of a Yankee legend, it was dèja vu all over again in the Bronx last night as Cam Schlittler continued crafting a legend of his own. Just like last season, Schlittler delivered a gem of a performance against the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, staking New York to a 1-0 series lead and giving them an opportunity to close the affair out early tonight. But unlike last year's three-game set, in which the Yankee offense never fully erupted, the lineup finally achieved escape velocity. Be
item.content:encoded:
In the words of a Yankee legend, it was dèja vu all over again in the Bronx last night as Cam Schlittler continued crafting a legend of his own. Just like last season, Schlittler delivered a gem of a performance against the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, staking New York to a 1-0 series lead and giving them an opportunity to close the affair out early tonight. But unlike last year's three-game set, in which the Yankee offense never fully erupted, the lineup finally achieved escape velocity. Ben Rice and his four hits, two homers, and six RBI, led the charge — but the bottom of the lineup contributed their fair share as well.
In other words, the Yankees played the perfect ballgame last night. Max Fried will be tasked with carrying the momentum into Game 2. Fried's second season in pinstripes has been marred by a couple of IL stints limiting him to just 20 starts and 112.2 innings, but when he's been healthy, he's been just as good as in 2025. He'll be pitching on seven days' rest in Game 2 — his last appearance was an up-and-down start against the Rays, in which Tampa clinched the AL East.
As far as the recent track record against Boston, Fried has been quite effective. He only faced them twice this season: one was a short start from when he was returning from his latest injury, the other an eight-inning masterpiece in April from before the Red Sox got it together under new manager Chad Tracy. In Game 1 of last year's WCS, he provided 6.1 scoreless innings, scattering four hits three walks while striking out six. The Yankees couldn't hold onto the narrow 1-0 lead he had defended, and sabotaged their own comeback effort after loading the bases with nobody out in the ninth inning. None of that was Max's fault, of course. Provided the lineup supports him, an effort like last year's will be more than enough.
Old friend Sonny Gray never caught on with the Yankees in 2017 and 2018, but he'll have no choice but to step up under the Yankee Stadium lights with Boston's season on the line. Over his first season with the Red Sox, the steady veteran turned in yet another outstanding season, leading the AL with 18 wins (don't think that doesn't mean anything to him) and pitching to a 2.72 ERA. That's the thing about the Red Sox' pitching: they have lots of exciting youngsters like Payton Tolle, who pitched last night, but they also routinely get the most out of their veteran pitchers too. Gray faced New York twice in June and pitched well both times. The latter outing was his best start of the season by game score — one hit, one walk, nine strikeouts over 7.1 scoreless innings.
Unsurprisingly, Aaron Boone's lineup for Game 2 is nearly unrecognizable when compared with the Game 1 starting nine. It's a history-making card: according to James Smyth of the YES Network, it's the first time a team has put eight lefty batters — switch hitters not included — in the same lineup in the postseason. The portside octet includes Trent Grisham, who entered late last night for his first action off the IL. Rice will ascend to the leadoff spot, with Cody Bellinger and Luis Garcia Jr. to follow. Spencer Jones hits cleanup and plays right field ahead of George Lombard Jr., the lone righty to get the start. Jazz Chisholm Jr. draws in at the keystone, Grisham bats in the seven-spot after him, Austin Wells will bat eighth, and Ryan McMahon starts at third and will hit ninth. Naturally, expect plenty of right-handed bats to come off the bench against a lefty-heavy Boston staff once Gray's start concludes.
How to watch
Location: Yankee Stadium – Bronx, NY
First pitch: 8:00 p.m. ET
TV broadcast: NBC
Radio broadcast: WFAN 660/101.9 FM, WADO 1280 (NYY) | WEEI 93.7, WCCM 1490 AM (SP), WESX 1230 AM (SP) (BOS) | ESPN Radio (national)
Streaming: Peacock

item.dc:creator: Mike Cronin
item.description: Roman Anthony out of Red Sox lineup for Game 2 of Wild Card Series The Red Sox season will rest on the arm of starting pitcher Sonny Gray as the team takes on the New York Yankees on Wednesday in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series. item.content:encoded:
Roman Anthony out of Red Sox lineup for Game 2 of Wild Card Series
The Red Sox season will rest on the arm of starting pitcher Sonny Gray as the team takes on the New York Yankees on Wednesday in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series.
The Sox won't have the services of Roman Anthony, who appeared to reaggravate his hand injury during the team's 9-0 loss in Game 1.
"We actually sent him back to Boston last evening to get there so he could be early in the morning and re-image the hand, which shows additional damage to some muscles in his wrist that weren't there before," Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said. "So he's sore and obviously not in the lineup."
Anthony will be replaced on the roster by infielder Curtis Mead, who broke his wrist during his debut with the Red Sox on July 27. Anthony would eligible to return to the lineup for the American League Championship Series.
The Sox will have long odds to beat to continue their playoff run. Teams taking a 1-0 lead in a three-game wild-card series have gone on to win that series 21 out of 24 times, 17 times with a sweep.
Home teams have won all nine series in which they have won the first game.
On Tuesday, Yankees starter Cam Schlittler and the rest of the pitching staff held the Sox to just three hits.
Red Sox starting pitcher Payton Tolle might have been the team's best player, but manager Chad Tracy pulled him in the fifth inning of a 1-run game. Reliever Erik Miller immediately gave up a homer to Dartmouth College graduate Ben Rice, and it was all downhill from there.
On Wednesday night, Gray will pitch opposite Yankees starter Max Fried.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Red Sox must hope Sonny Gray justifies their choice with Ranger Suarez's playoff pedigree looming
item.dc:creator: Brian Burrows
item.description: It's do-or-die for the Boston Red Sox in Game 2 of the Wild Card series. Game 1 was a disaster — while Payton Tolle was able to hold the New York Yankees to one run in his 4 ⅔ innings, it really didn't matter because the offense couldn't get anything going the entire game. They now head into Game 2 with one thing in mind: put runs on the board. The offense will need to find something against Max Fried, and they are going to need the pitching staff to keep them in the game as best it can. Sonny G
item.content:encoded:
It's do-or-die for the Boston Red Sox in Game 2 of the Wild Card series. Game 1 was a disaster — while Payton Tolle was able to hold the New York Yankees to one run in his 4 ⅔ innings, it really didn't matter because the offense couldn't get anything going the entire game.
They now head into Game 2 with one thing in mind: put runs on the board. The offense will need to find something against Max Fried, and they are going to need the pitching staff to keep them in the game as best it can. Sonny Gray will take the bump for the Sox in the pivotal matchup, but he may be the wrong choice.
Over the offseason, the Red Sox made two big pitching acquisitions: Gray and Ranger Suarez. Gray was a veteran who was essentially in the last year of his deal, meant to be a mid-rotation arm. Suarez was meant to be the No. 2 behind Garrett Crochet, and his playoff excellence was supposed to help after what the Red Sox starters struggled (besides Crochet) in the Wild Card last year.
Recency bias is influencing the Red Sox's starter decision for Game 2 of the Wild Card
Suarez is one of the best playoff pitchers in baseball ever. His 1.48 ERA in the postseason is the sixth-lowest for any pitcher with 40 or more playoff innings pitched. He has held hitters to a .201 batting average while striking out over nine per nine innings. His numbers in the regular season are great, but the selling point was what he could do in October.
Now, of course, the regular season played a part in the decision to start Gray in Game 2. The righty was dominant all year and could finish in the top five in Cy Young voting. Gray had a 2.72 ERA this season over 169 innings. It's hard not to guarantee a pitcher who performed so well in the regular season a start in the postseason when he was so influential in getting the team there. But Suarez is on the team for this exact moment.
In a win-or-go-home scenario, it's hard not to hand the ball to the pitcher who slows his heartbeat in the playoffs. If the Sox can win this game, it will be great to have Suarez pitching Game 3, but the Red Sox need to keep themselves in the game. Gray could be the one to do it, but the track record says Suarez is the better choice.

item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox are in danger of watching their season come to a close in Yankee Stadium for the second consecutive year. The offense showed zero signs of life as the Yankees cruised to a 9-0 victory headlined by 10 strikeouts from growing Red Sox killer Cam Schlittler. Payton Tolle did enough on the mound as the Game 1 starter. His team was clearly just unable to do their part around them.
Now, the Red Sox fall into the need of a historic response given that just 3 of 24 teams to lose the opener in the Wild Card round have come back to win the series. For starters, Boston sends 18-game winner Sonny Gray to the mound. He flirted with a no-hitter the last time he faced New York in June and tallied a 1.98 ERA against the Yankees in 2026.
The Yankees counter with Max Fried, who has battled some inconsistencies in his ramp-up period from an injury return. The southpaw does have a sparkling 1.93 career ERA against the Red Sox in addition to a brilliant start in Game 1 last year with 6 1/3 scoreless innings, which his bullpen ruined in Boston's 3-1 victory. To best combat the talented lefty, Jahmai Jones slots in leading off as the designated hitter. Caleb Durbin moves up to the sixth spot and Nate Eaton – another right-handed bat – gets the nod in left field.
After being shut out in consecutive postseason games, the Red Sox must find a way to score runs and now do so without Roman Anthony, who will come off the ALWC roster with new and aggravated injuries in his right hand. It's an uphill challenge undoubtedly, though it's one Boston must be ready for in order to extend the season.

Yankees:

item.title: [New York Post] Chad Tracy’s controversial call to pull Payton Tolle backfired for Red Sox in horrific fashion in Game 1 blowout
item.dc:creator: Matt Ehalt
item.description: Payton Tolle had just retired Paul Goldschmidt for the third time on one pitch, running his pitch count to a manageable 83 with two outs in the fifth inning Tuesday, when Chad Tracy decided he’d seen enough. With Boston trailing by one run and Ben Rice, who doubled in the first inning, due up next, the manager opted to remove his pitcher who had settled into the pitching duel by that point. And it backfired in horrible fashion for Boston. Lefty reliever Erik Miller immediately surrendered a long
item.content:encoded:
Payton Tolle had just retired Paul Goldschmidt for the third time on one pitch, running his pitch count to a manageable 83 with two outs in the fifth inning Tuesday, when Chad Tracy decided he’d seen enough.
With Boston trailing by one run and Ben Rice, who doubled in the first inning, due up next, the manager opted to remove his pitcher who had settled into the pitching duel by that point.
And it backfired in horrible fashion for Boston.
Lefty reliever Erik Miller immediately surrendered a long solo homer to center field to Rice — the first of his two against Boston relievers — and it completely changed the tone of the game in Boston’s 9-0 loss to the Yankees in Game 1 of the AL Wild Card series at Yankee Stadium.
Boston’s b-tier relievers ultimately surrendered eight runs in 3 1/3 innings.
“Not just the pitch count necessarily, but you’re trailing already, you’re moving through the third time,” Tracy said. “Rice had already hit a double in the gap off of him, and you have a nice lane there for Miller, and obviously he got him. Just felt like it was the time to go.”
This postseason marks Tracy’s first calling the shots and moments like this one Tuesday night are what ultimately can swing series.
Sure, Boston did not score, but being down 1-0 to Cam Schlittler and the Yankees bullpen is a vastly different world than trailing by two entering the seventh.
Tolle allowed four hits over the first nine batters but settled down to retire eight of the next 10 batters and navigated a two-on, no-outs situation in the fifth while trailing 1-0.
He began the sixth by retiring Austin Wells on six pitches and then sitting down Goldschmidt, leaving him certainly with room to possibly navigate six innings if he worked effectively.
Tracy, though, opted for a new look in Miller, ending Tolle’s day after 4 2/3 innings of one-run ball.
“I thought he threw the ball well,” Tracy said. “They did an effective job of grinding the count up as well. He had traffic. They put traffic on him. He was able to navigate his way through that. I think he competed extremely well for the time that he was out there and gave us what he could.
“I think the number being up there in the mid-80s, still trying to get through five, probably higher than what you normally see with Payton, and to be expected in an environment like this. But I thought he competed his butt off.”
Miller, a midseason trade acquisition, struggled to end the regular season and those issues carried over to the postseason when he fired a middle-middle 97-mph heater that Rice hit out to dead center.
Tolle said that as a competitor, he felt he could have gone longer but understood the decision due to the strength of Boston’s bullpen during the regular seaosn.
Boston is now one loss away from a second straight early postseason exit at the Yankees’ hands.
“Wasn’t good enough,” Tolle said. “They had a good plan and I threw a lot of balls … just didn’t feel like I could command the zone, kind of let some at-bats get away from me. A lot of pitches.”
He added about the bullpen: “Those guys picked me up a lot this year.”

Contreras was hit on the hand by a pitch against the Texas R
item.content:encoded:
After the Boston Red Sox went on their summer run to climb safely into an American League wild-card spot, that proved to be huge. Nobody can predict injuries, but it was a rough month of September in terms of injuries.
Not only did manager Chad Tracy lose Gold Glove outfielder Ceddanne Rafaela to an injury early in the month, but he also lost All-Star first baseman Willson Contreras to an injury with 10 days left in the regular season. Contreras was hit on the hand by a pitch against the Texas Rangers. He played in just one game after that.
He’ll be back in the Red Sox lineup for Game 1 of the AL wild-card series on Tuesday night against the New York Yankees. Boston is also getting Rafaela back in the Bronx, but the lineup will look different against Cam Schlittler.
Ceddanne Rafaela Batting Fifth in Game 1 vs. New York Yankees
Boston announced their lineup hours before Game 1 and Rafaela will be hitting fifth. Here is the lineup for the Red Sox,
Wilyer Abreu RF
Caddanne Rafaela CF
Nick Sogard 2B
Jarren Duran LF
Trevor Story SS
Caleb Durbin 3B
Rafaela was placed on the injured list with a right quadriceps strain, which caused him to miss 17 games. He returned against the Cleveland Guardians on Sept. 23 before exiting the game with right hamstring tightness while legging out a single. The next day, testing came back clean, and he was diagnosed with a hamstring cramp. He went 2-for-6 against the Guardians and Chicago Cubs in three games before the playoffs with a pair of singles.
Red Sox Big Wild Card Lead Led To Key Rest for Ceddanne Rafaela
If Rafaela can return and produce for Tracy, the big lead in the playoff race in the American League was huge. It allowed Boston to give not only Rafaela time to rest, but also Contreras as well.
Boston will be without utility infielder Mickey Gasper, who suffered an injury last Friday in Game 1 of a doubleheader against the Cubs at Fenway Park. He was placed on the 10-day injured list, which takes an underrated bat out of Tracy’s lineup and off his bench.
The Red Sox will send young left-hander Payton Tolle to the mound against the New York Yankees, who will send this lineup out for manager Aaron Boone,
Ben Rice DH
Heliot Ramos RF
George Lombard Jr. SS
Amed Rosario 3B
Anthony Vole 2B
New York won’t have Aaron Judge for the series, as he was not part of Boone’s roster. This figures to be a low-scoring series given the projected pitching matchups for the three games, if it goes that far. Boston getting Rafaela and Contreras back while the Yankees not having Judge feels like an advantage for the Red Sox. Winning Game 1 is big in a best-of-three series, especially for the Yankees, with Boston having Sonny Gray scheduled to go in Game 2 on Wednesday night.

item.title: [si.com] MLB Postseason Power Rankings: Strength and Weaknesses for Every Playoff Team
item.dc:creator: Karl Rasmussen
item.description: The postseason field is finally set. After Sunday’s results on the final day of the regular season, we officially know what 12 teams will be in contention for the 2026 World Series. The Diamondbacks, despite their late push, fell short of the playoffs, thanks to a Phillies win on Sunday against the Rays. Meanwhile, the final domino to fall in the American League went in favor of the Astros, who secured the AL West title with a victory over the Athletics on Sunday. Houston becomes the worst team
item.content:encoded:
The postseason field is finally set. After Sunday’s results on the final day of the regular season, we officially know what 12 teams will be in contention for the 2026 World Series.
The Diamondbacks, despite their late push, fell short of the playoffs, thanks to a Phillies win on Sunday against the Rays. Meanwhile, the final domino to fall in the American League went in favor of the Astros, who secured the AL West title with a victory over the Athletics on Sunday. Houston becomes the worst team to ever make the playoffs in a 162-game season, sneaking in and winning the division with just an 81–81 record.
Fans won’t have to wait long for postseason to get underway, with the Wild Card series set to begin on Tuesday. But before the action gets going, we’re going to do a final power ranking, assessing where all 12 teams sit and detailing their biggest strength and weakness.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
Biggest strength: Elite starting pitching, lineup
Biggest weakness: Bullpen
The Dodgers may be the No. 2 seed in the National League, but they’re built to win in October. It’s hard to determine what’s a greater strength between their loaded starting rotation or their star-studded lineup. There’s no weaknesses in their rotation, with All-Star caliber pitchers available to take the mound every night, even with Shohei Ohtani restricted to DH duties. There isn’t a team in MLB with more postseason experience than Los Angeles, who have won back-to-back World Series with this core. During the regular season, the Dodgers had MLB’s second-highest OPS (.762) and fourth-best ERA (3.55). If there’s any way to beat them it’s by getting after a bullpen that has been inconsistent throughout the season, though it’s still a top-10 unit. Injuries have plagued their relief pitching corps, however, with the likes of Blake Treinen, Edgardo Henriquez and Will Klein all currently on IL.
2. Milwaukee Brewers
Biggest strength: Elite pitching
Biggest weakness: Lack of power
The Brewers’ rotation, headlined by NL Cy Young favorite Jacob Misiorowski, has been one of MLB’s best, and it’s helped the team secure the league’s best regular-season record. The starting rotation owns MLB’s fifth-best ERA (3.65) and their bullpen has been equally impressive, ranking third in MLB with a 3.40 ERA. Milwaukee has scored the second-most runs in the league this season (832), as their small-ball approach has worked wonders for them. But in October, when a single swing of the bat can dramatically change a team’s fortunes and rallies are harder to come by, they might not have the power hitters capable of providing that big home run swing. The Brewers didn’t have a single 30-home run hitter this season and had just three everyday starters with a slugging percentage above .450.
3. Tampa Bay Rays
Biggest strength: Elite starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Bottom-third of the lineup
The Rays had the best record in the American League this season, largely thanks to their pitching. The starting rotation has been excellent, ranking third in MLB with a 3.51 ERA. Drew Rasmussen has quietly been one of MLB’s best arms, and Freddy Peralta has begun to rediscover his previous form after a rough go with the Mets and a shaky start on the mound in Tampa. Much like the Brewers, the Rays primarily utilize a small-ball approach offensively. The Rays hit the ninth-fewest home runs in MLB this year, and despite rostering some elite hitters such as Junior Caminero and Yandy Diaz, they haven’t received much production out of the bottom third of their lineup, which is their biggest weakness with the postseason looming.
4. Atlanta Braves
Biggest strength: Deep lineup
Biggest weakness: Plate discipline, low on-base rates
The Braves are another team with an abundance of postseason experience in the lineup. They have several players that can turn a game on its head with one swing of the bat, and had five 20-plus home run hitters during the regular season in Matt Olson, Michael Harris, Drake Baldwin, Ozzie Albies and Ronald Acuña Jr. Although the lineup is flush with talent, the group has a tendency to chase pitches out of the zone, and they don’t draw walks at a high rate. The Braves ranked 28th in MLB in on-base percentage (.309) during the regular season, often opting for an aggressive approach at the plate rather than a patient one. That could prove costly in October against some of the best pitchers in the sport, where slowing the game down and getting runners on base by any means necessary will be crucial.
5. New York Yankees
Biggest strength: Elite pitching rotation
Biggest weakness: Offense (without Aaron Judge), high strikeout rates
Yankees starting pitchers led MLB with a 3.30 ERA this season, and they’ll have one of the best rotations in the postseason with Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodon set to take the mound in October. The bullpen has been a bit inconsistent, but they should be able to ride their starting rotation deep into games. The biggest weakness for the Yankees is their lineup, particularly without Aaron Judge in the mix. New York had the sixth-most strikeouts this season and were tied for 11th in MLB with a .720 OPS. With Judge out of the lineup, however, their OPS falls to a .690 mark, which would be 29th in MLB.
6. San Diego Padres
Biggest strength: Elite bullpen
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The Padres’ bullpen has been as reliable as they come this season, and the team flexes multiple elite relievers who they can reliably turn the ball over to in the later innings in Mason Miller, Yuki Matsui and Adrian Morejon, among others. San Diego has shaken off a slow start to the year and are playing at an extremely high level heading into the postseason. The offense is alive again after a dreadful first couple of months of the season, with players like Fernando Tatis Jr. and Jackson Merrill having been among MLB’s best second-half performers at the plate. The starting pitching will be the x-factor in October, however. With Casey Mize landing on the IL, their options in the rotation are even thinner. Remaining competitive within the first six innings will be crucial for the Padres, whose starting pitchers rank 21st in MLB with a 4.42 ERA this year.
7. Chicago Cubs
Biggest strength: Dominant lineup
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The Cubs have had MLB’s best offense this season, leading the league in OPS (.767), walks (674), runs scored (850) and slugging percentage (.428). They’ve been particularly elite since the All-Star break, logging a .797 OPS in their last 66 games. With Pete Crow-Armstrong playing at an MVP level and Alex Bregman having enjoyed a monster second half, the Cubs’ offense will be tough to shut down in October. Of course, they’ll need their pitching to live up to their end of the bargain, which it’s struggled to do this season. Chicago’s starting pitching has been disappointing and plagued by injuries. The starting rotation ranks 18th in MLB with a 4.27 ERA this year and have surrendered the third-most home runs (142).
8. Boston Red Sox
Biggest strength: Elite pitching
Biggest weakness: Inconsistent offense
The Red Sox’s pitching as a whole has been excellent. Boston’s bullpen owns a league-best 3.00 ERA this season, and no group of relievers in MLB has surrendered fewer home runs (55). Their starters have been great, too, ranking eighth in the league with a 3.92 ERA, and they boast a solid mix of veterans (Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez) and young, emerging starters (Payton Tolle and Jake Bennett). Offensively, however, the Red Sox have been prone to spells of inconsistency. They started the season ice cold before enjoying a scalding hot summer streak, but they’ve come crashing back down to earth in the final month of the season. The Red Sox rank dead last in MLB in OPS (.651) throughout the month of September, and they’re batting a league-worst .219 in that span.
9. Cleveland Guardians
Biggest strength: Starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Lack of power
The Guardians starting pitching has been a top-10 unit this season, ranking ninth in ERA (3.93) and fifth in strikeouts (878). Parker Messick has been superb in his first full season in MLB, and Gavin Williams has emerged as one of the league’s best strikeout pitchers. Cleveland will feel confident with those two spearheading the rotation, but they may struggle to get the run support required to take advantage of their quality starters. The Guardians rank 24th in MLB with 678 runs scored, 26th in OPS (.696) and 27th in home runs (162) this season. If they can’t come up with some big at-bats, it won’t matter how effective their pitching is in October.
10. Philadelphia Phillies
Biggest strength: Starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Defense, bullpen
The Phillies have one of the best starting rotations in MLB, but they’ve been plagued by some underperforming position players and a lackluster bullpen. There’s arguably no better trio of starters in MLB than Cristopher Sánchez, Zack Wheeler and Jesús Luzardo. The team’s starting rotation ranks seventh in the league with a 3.80 ERA, but their bullpen ranks 21st in ERA (4.43). Defensively, the Phillies have been atrocious, too. Only the Athletics have fewer defensive runs saved than the Phillies’ -43, according to the Fielding Bible, and the infield has been a serious concern, with Trea Turner, Bryce Harper and Alec Bohm all ranking among the bottom 26 defensive players (of 270 qualified players) in MLB in terms of outs above average, per Statcast. Defensive shortcomings and mishaps could prove highly costly in October, and that’s an area that’s plagued Philadelphia all season.
11. Chicago White Sox
Biggest strength: Power hitting
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The White Sox have a potent lineup and are the only team in MLB that have three players who hit 30 or more home runs in Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami and Colson Montgomery. Chicago hit the fifth-most home runs this season (211) and scored the fifth-most runs (776). While the offense is among the league’s best in terms of power, the White Sox starting pitching is a serious concern. The starting rotation posted a season ERA of 4.60 (fourth-worst in MLB), a 1.34 WHIP (sixth-worst in MLB) and recorded the third-fewest strikeouts of any starting rotation in the league. Chicago’s starters also threw the fewest innings in MLB this season, often struggling to get deep into games before the baton was passed to the bullpen. If the starting rotation can’t keep runs off the board, it might not matter how explosive their lineup can be.
12. Houston Astros
Biggest strength: Power hitting
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
Yordan Alvarez is likely to win the AL MVP, and he’s the type of hitter teams will not be eager to pitch to in October. No team in MLB hit more home runs than the Astros, who hit 226. In addition to Alvarez’s 42, Houston had four other players with 20-plus homers, including Christian Walker (29), Isaac Paredes (25), Jeremy Peña (22) and Cam Smith (21). They don’t have much to worry about offensively, but their lineup will need to produce in order to ease the burden on their starting rotation, which has largely struggled this year. Hunter Brown remains a reliable ace, but beyond him there’s a lack of experience and talent within the rotation. Astros starters ranked 27th in MLB with a 4.81 ERA and 1.40 WHIP, both of which were the worst among all teams that qualified for the postseason, and they walked the most batters in MLB this season. If the lineup can’t make up for the rotation’s shortcomings, it could be a short postseason stint for Houston this year.
Karl Rasmussen is a staff writer for Sports Illustrated. A University of Oregon alum who joined SI in February 2023, his work has appeared on 12up and ClutchPoints. Rasmussen is a loyal Tottenham, Jets, Yankees and Ducks fan.
Follow Karlras920

item.title: [Over the Monster] Chad Tracy could swing the series between the Red Sox and Yankees
item.dc:creator: Keagan Stiefel
item.description: Chad Tracy is hardly the only person that has been added to the fold between the Boston Red Sox and New York Yankees’ back-to-back meetings in the American League Wild Card Series. The Red Sox have made substantial additions to the rotation, with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez being named the starting pitchers for the best-of-three series at Yankee Stadium — making for a much deeper unit than the one that fell off a cliff after Garrett Crochet last season and relied on the likes of
item.content:encoded:
Chad Tracy is hardly the only person that has been added to the fold between the Boston Red Sox and New York Yankees’ back-to-back meetings in the American League Wild Card Series.
The Red Sox have made substantial additions to the rotation, with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez being named the starting pitchers for the best-of-three series at Yankee Stadium — making for a much deeper unit than the one that fell off a cliff after Garrett Crochet last season and relied on the likes of Brayan Bello and Connelly Early. Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman, and Caleb Durbin will join the lineup in hopes to scrape together more than the six total runs they scored last season. Crochet could end up joining the bullpen in his return from injury, along with newcomers Erik Miller and Jake Bennett, which is a pretty decent group of pitchers being added to one of the very best units in baseball this season.
The Yankees will also be in a better position on the pitching side, with Gerrit Cole serving as the do-or-die option behind Cam Schlittler and Max Fried. Luis Garcia Jr., Heliot Ramos, and George Lombard Jr. should help the lineup against left-handers, though there is something to be said about the so-so status of Aaron Judge.
If we can boil all of that down, though, only one man can completely swing the series…
Chad Tracy.
Tracy’s most difficult decisions might come before the season even starts, as he will be relied upon heavily to figure out who will fill out the roster — Braiden Ward? Jarren Duran? Curtis Mead? Jahmai Jones? Nate Eaton? Isiah Kiner-Falefa? Crochet?
It’s not going to be easy, but all of that pales in comparison to making decisions with who will play, when they will play, and how he manages things when the lights are at their brightest in The Bronx.
“It’s the playoffs, so we’re at the point in the season where teams that are remaining need to win or they’re going home,” Tracy said during his media availability on Monday. “I have a feel for that.
“… It’s all hands on deck. I think everyone is aware that during the playoffs it’s about winning moments and being aggressive — all those things. I think most of our guys who have been around understand that, so we’re going to go out and play our butts off and manage and do everything we can to win each game.”
Alex Cora, the manager of last year’s squad that became the first in history to lose the best-of-three series after taking a lead, made some… interesting decisions in hindsight.
Bello was pulled after 2 1/3 innings in Game 2, which led to Justin Wilson, Zack Kelly, Garrett Whitlock, and Tolle being used out of the bullpen and becoming unavailable for Game 3. Nate Eaton started over Wilyer Abreu in Game 2. Rob Refsnyder got two starts over Masataka Yoshida, which makes sense considering they faced two left-handers, but he finished 0-for-5 while the latter went 4-for-7. Nathaniel Lowe played in all three games, while Nick Sogard only played in two.
It’s easy to go back in time and poke holes though these decisions with the benefit of hindsight, but that’s kind of the whole point in looking ahead at the same two teams playing each other again with one of them being led by someone new.
Tracy needs to avoid making similar mistakes, and he needs to do it without the benefit of years of experience in similar situations. The Red Sox stripped him of that interim tag because they believe he can, and it’s only a matter of time before we find out whether or not they’re right.

Abridores para la serie Yankees vs. Red So
item.content:encoded:
Yankees y Red Sox revelan a sus pitchers abridores para la Serie de Comodines
Yankees y Red Sox se enfrentan por segundo año consecutivo al comenzar la postemporada de la MLB.
Velando armas para una nueva batalla en la que ambos se juegan la temporada, Yankees y Red Sox anunciaron a sus pitchers abridores con los que se enfrentarán a partir de este martes en una nueva Serie de Comodines para abrir los Playoffs 2026 en las Grandes Ligas de Béisbol (MLB).
Abridores para la serie Yankees vs. Red Sox
- Juego 1: Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.03) vs. Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95)
- Juego 2: Sonny Gray (18-5, 2.72) vs. Max Fried (5-5, 2.80)
- Juego 3: Ranger Suárez (8-5, 3.22) vs. Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61)
Juego 1: Cam Schlittler vs. Payton Tolle
Los Yankees apostaron todo al alinear a Cam Schlittler, el principal contendiente para competir por el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana, para el Juego 1. Schlittler, quien creció a los alrededores de Boston siendo un aficionado de los Red Sox, fue el verdugo del equipo de su infancia el año anterior cuando tiró 8.0 entradas de 12 ponches para ganar el decisivo Juego 3.
Esta temporada, Schlittler tuvo efectividad de 0.74 pues apenas recibió dos carreras limpias a lo largo de 24.1 entradas ante los Red Sox este año, aunque admitió 4 carreras inmerecidas el 25 de junio.
Su antagonista será Payton Tolle, el novato zurdo que tomará por asalto la lomita del Yankee Stadium. Con 23 años y 332 días de edad, Tolle será el tercer pitcher más joven en abrir una serie de postemporada para los Red Sox. En dos actuaciones ante los Yankees, Payton tuvo marca de 1-0 con efectividad de 0.69 y 18 ponches, a cambio de solo tres pasaportes.
Juego 2: Max Fried vs Sonny Gray
Sonny Gray tomará la pelota para el Juego 2 por los Red Sox. El as en la rotación en la ausencia de Garrett Crochet tuvo un año increíble y busca trasladar ese éxito a la postemporada ante unos Yankees a los que dominó en dos aperturas: la primera en 6.1 entradas de 3 carreras, mientras que en la segunda tiró una joya de 7.1 entradas en un solo hit y 9 ponches.
Los Yankees optaron por Max Fried en el Juego 2, otro lanzador que fue dominante ante los Red Sox la postemporada anterior tirando 6.1 entradas en blanco pese a admitir 4 hits y regalar 3 bases por bolas; ponchó a 6 rivales. Desde entonces, Fried acumula 18.0 entradas de una sola carrera y 19 ponches ante los acérrimos rivales de los Bombarderos del Bronx.
Juego 3: Gerrit Cole vs. Ranger Suárez
En caso de un decisivo Juego 3, los Yankees saltarán al terreno con Gerrit Cole, el lanzador que históricamente ha sufrido ante los Red Sox. Cole no le ha ganado un juego a Boston desde el 17 de julio de 2022 y su efectividad de por vida ante los patirrojos es de 5.30, la segunda más alta que tiene ante cualquier rival, solo debajo de los Mets (7.28).
Ranger Suárez cerró fuerte para ganarse la confianza y ser el abridor de los Red Sox para el Juego 3 de esta Serie de Comodines. Durante el último mes de temporada en su año de debut con los Red Sox, el venezolano Suárez cerró con marca de 3-1 y efectividad de 1.09 en septiembre; sin embargo, ante los Yankees fue sumamente contrastante al admitir 10 carreras en 10.0 entradas de dos juegos que perdió y 6.1 entradas de una carrera en un juego sin decisión.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] If the Red Sox can get past the Yankees, the Chad Tracy story goes from a good one to a great one - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Peter Abraham
item.description: NEW YORK — Because there are odds on everything these days, Will Venable is the favorite to be the American League Manager of the Year, with Kevin Cash the second choice. Venable led the White Sox to the postseason after losing 102 games last season. He deserves all the plaudits. But what about Chad Tracy? item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — Because there are odds on everything these days, Will Venable is the favorite to be the American League Manager of the Year, with Kevin Cash the second choice.
Venable led the White Sox to the postseason after losing 102 games last season. He deserves all the plaudits.
But what about Chad Tracy?
Tracy was called away from managing a game with Triple-A Worcester on April 25 and told that Alex Cora was getting fired and he would manage the Red Sox the next day in Baltimore. It was the baseball equivalent of getting thrown out of a plane without a parachute.
After making the announcement, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow said he couldn’t guarantee Tracy would finish the season as manager.
Five months later, the Sox are in the playoffs after a remarkable turnaround, and Tracy is the only rookie manager whose team is still playing.
It’s a good story, complete with Tracy agreeing to a three-year contract last week. But in two or three more days, it could be a great story.
The Sox have not won a postseason series since 2021. If they fall to the Yankees again this season, nothing will have changed. But if they beat their rivals and advance to the Division Series, it’s a major step forward for this largely unaccomplished group of players.
“It’s drastically different,” Tracy said Monday when asked to compare becoming manager to managing in his first postseason game. “It’s the playoffs. There’s more riding on it.”
Tracy said he gave himself some grace that first day in Baltimore. There was so much to learn, so much to do. He knew he wouldn’t be fully prepared. Plus, several of the players were still furious that Cora had been fired after only 27 games.
“It was go out and be with the guys and give them a hug and enjoy being with them and let the game go be what it is,” Tracy said.
Tracy leaned on his father for advice throughout the season. Jim Tracy managed 1736 major league games from 2001-12 for three teams and had plenty of good answers. But he was 2-6 in postseason games, losing first-round series with the 2004 Dodgers and 2009 Rockies.
As a manager’s son, Tracy suffered those losses, too.
“This is the playoffs. We’re at the point in the season for the teams that are remaining where it’s a three-game series. You’ve got to win the series or you go home,” he said. “There’s more riding on it.”
For 162 games, managers are forced to think about the next day, the next series, and the next set of roster moves. Bruised egos get massaged, and you move on. Even great teams lose dozens of games. That’s baseball.
Not in the playoffs. Everything goes into winning that day, and feelings are disregarded. Just win.
“When you get to this part of the year, it’s all hands on deck. I think everybody’s pretty aware in the playoffs it’s high intent and winning moments and being aggressive and all those things,” Tracy said.
“All of our guys that have been around understand that. They’re going to play their butts off, and we’re going to manage and try to do whatever we can to win the game.”
That would be the case if the Sox were playing the Astros. But it’s magnified by the power of 100 when it’s the Yankees.
The Sox made history against the Yankees with their comeback in the 2004 American League Championship Series. They brushed past the Bombers in the division round en route to the 2018 championship. Fenway Park was practically shaking during the 2021 Wild Card game.
“I don’t like to give that way more attention than it needs. But I won’t shy away from it,” Tracy said. “Two historic franchises, big rivalry, well aware of that.”
Tracy has already made one bold move, selecting Payton Tolle as his Game 1 starter instead of the more seasoned Sonny Gray. More big decisions are coming.
There’s no grace now.
Peter Abraham can be reached at peter.abraham@globe.com. Follow him on Bluesky at peteabeglobe.bsky.social.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Biggest Takeaways from Chad Tracy's Pre-Postseason Media Availability
item.dc:creator: Zach Coe
item.description: RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses some roster decisions to keep an eye on ahead of the postseason rosters finalizing on the 'Entering Kenmore' Podcast. Subscribe on YouTube and be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com! The Boston Red Sox have arrived in New York ahead of their Wild Card series against the New York Yankees, which begins Tuesday night (8:00 p.m. ET). Before taking the field to determine who advances to a divisional-round series against the Tampa Bay Rays
item.content:encoded:
RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses some roster decisions to keep an eye on ahead of the postseason rosters finalizing on the 'Entering Kenmore' Podcast. Subscribe on YouTube and be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
The Boston Red Sox have arrived in New York ahead of their Wild Card series against the New York Yankees, which begins Tuesday night (8:00 p.m. ET). Before taking the field to determine who advances to a divisional-round series against the Tampa Bay Rays, both teams were made available to the media Monday afternoon at Yankee Stadium.
Here's what you need to know about Red Sox manager Chad Tracy's media availability:
Payton Tolle further cements his status as a budding ace
The big story of Tracy's availability was the announcement of the starting rotation for the series, headlined by 23-year-old rookie Payton Tolle taking the mound in Tuesday's Game 1. Tolle has already established himself as one of baseball's best young arms, putting together a rookie campaign that should see him finish in the top three in American League Rookie of the Year voting.
Even with Tolle's regular-season success, few, if any, other 23-year-old rookies would be trusted to take the mound in Game 1 of a postseason series in an environment as hostile as Yankee Stadium.
"Just felt like with his power stuff that was the best choice for Game 1," Tracy said of the decision to start Tolle. "I know his age; I know he's a rookie, but as far as he approaches baseball and big moments, that part won't bother him. He's a pretty special personality... he's just going to go out there and pitch his game regardless of what it is," he continued.
Tolle has earned the trust and respect of his teammates and coaching staff, and they feel confident in his ability to go head-to-head with the likely American League Cy Young Award winner, Yankees starter Cam Schlittler, which is a real testament to his future as the Red Sox' ace.
Garrett Crochet's status remains up in the air
Speaking of Cy Young-caliber pitchers, the 2025 AL Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet traveled with the team to New York after throwing a live bullpen in Ft. Myers on Saturday. Despite being with the team, Crochet's status for the Wild Card round remains up in the air as the team continues to monitor his left shoulder's recovery after each day of work.
In order to activate Crochet, the Red Sox brass will have several questions they'll need to answer: most importantly, how many games would Crochet be available to pitch in? While an arm like Crochet's in the bullpen could be a massive weapon for Tracy, if he can only pitch once in the three-game set, would the roster spot be better served by a pitcher who can give you multiple appearances?
"If we're able to activate [Crochet], obviously he's available, right? But I think beyond that, if we were to use him, the availability- whether that be the next day- would still be contingent on us continuing to evaluate him," Tracy said of Crochet's potential availability.
With Tyron Guerrero injured and out for at least the first two rounds of the postseason, creating a major hole in the back end of the Boston bullpen, it would be a relative surprise to see Crochet not on the Wild Card roster.
Willson Contreras will return to first base
After a pitch hit him in the hand in Boston's 4-3 win over the Texas Rangers on Sept. 17, Red Sox All-Star first baseman Willson Contreras cast doubt on his postseason availability after Thursday's series finale against the Cleveland Guardians. However, the 34-year-old returned to the lineup for Sunday's regular-season finale against the Chicago Cubs, logging two at-bats as the designated hitter.
Tracy told reporters that Contreras' inclusion in the lineup as DH was simply to give him some live reps in a game and that, as long as he checks out well after Monday's workouts, the plan was for him to return to first base Tuesday night.
Braiden Ward remains an option to make the roster
One of the Red Sox' most underrated moves made ahead of the trade deadline was an under-the-radar deal made with the Atlanta Braves to acquire outfielder Eli White. The 32-year-old was set to serve a crucial role on the postseason roster as the fourth outfielder and pinch-running specialist. However, those plans were cut short when White sustained a torn ligament in his right foot on Sept. 8, requiring surgery that ended his season.
As a result of White's injury, the door opened for spring-training standout Braiden Ward, who set a Triple-A club record for most stolen bases in a single season, to join the club for his big-league debut as a base-running specialist.
The 27-year-old is with the club in New York, but Tracy cautioned reporters not to read too much into his presence, as the roster is still being worked through.
Up next for the Sox
After weeks of discussion about what felt like an inevitable postseason matchup, the two rivals will take the field at Yankee Stadium on Tuesday night to kick off the best-of-three series. Tolle (9-6, 3.03 ERA) gets the start for Boston opposite Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA) for New York. First pitch is set for 8:00 p.m. ET.
For more on the Wild Card series
Zach Coe and David Azer are back on the 'Entering Kenmore' Podcast, previewing the Red Sox' Wild Card matchup with the Yankees. Check it out wherever you get your podcasts or in the YouTube player below.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are taking on the New York Yankees in an American League wild-card series beginning Tuesday, Sept. 29. Two teams with the most historic rivalry in baseball history square off with a chance to send the other home.
New York eliminated Boston in 2025, but with a new set of faces this year the Red Sox hope the result will be different.
One of those new faces is left-hander Payton Tolle. While Tolle debuted back in 2025 and appeared in the playoff series, he only made one appearance out of the bullpen. That will not be the case this time around.
Chad Tracy names wild-card series starters
Red Sox manager Chad Tracy spoke with reporters ahead of Game 1 and officially announced the rotation for Boston, per Bryan Hoch of MLB.com.
Tracy said Tolle gets the ball for Game 1, with veterans Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez to follow in that order. That represents a completely different look than what the Yankees saw last year, as both Gray and Suarez were added this offseason.
It makes plenty of sense that Tolle gets the ball. The 23-year-old has posted a 3.03 ERA across 26 starts and has piled up 171 strikeouts in 148 2/3 innings. Tolle has been superb in the second half and earned this moment.
Gray will get the ball for Game 2 and has been exactly as advertised in his first year with Boston. The 36-year-old veteran has posted a 2.72 ERA across 29 starts and has continued to age gracefully.
Suarez getting the ball third was the obvious choice as well. He has plenty of postseason experience from his time with the Philadelphia Phillies, and across 28 starts this year he has posted a 3.22 ERA with 140 strikeouts in 148 1/3 innings of work.
Boston’s lineup will have its work cut out against New York’s excellent rotation, but the Red Sox have the arms this year to match up against the Yankees in a way they simply did not a year ago.
Game 1 of the series is set for 8 p.m. ET Tuesday on NBC and Peacock.

item.title: [mlb.com] Tolle to kick off WC Series for Red Sox; Gray earns Game 2 start

item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox will start left-hander Payton Tolle in Game 1 of their American League Wild Card Series against the Yankees in New York on Tuesday night, manager Chad Tracy announced on Monday afternoon. Righty Sonny Gray, a former Yankee, will take the ball for Boston in Game 2.
Tolle, a rookie, has become a fireballing fan favorite in Boston, just as likely to strike someone out on a 98 mph heater as he is to wrap someone into a bear hug. The Red Sox have no reservations about putting the 23-year-old into the hostile territory Yankee Stadium figures to be.
The Yankees strongly considered left-hander Max Fried (5-5, 2.80 ERA) to start Game 1, but ultimately chose AL Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler for the opener. Fried will follow in Game 2, with Gerrit Cole ready for Game 3, if necessary.

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said Payton Tolle will start Game 1 of the Wild Card series against the Yankees.

Sonny Gray will start Game 2, with Ranger Suarez potentially lined up for Game 3. It seems that Tracy may be looking to break up his lefties. Tolle is certainly a worthwhile Game 1 starter. He finished the regular season with a 3.03 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, and 28.4 percent strikeout rate across 148 2/3 innings. He has never made a start in the postseason before, while Gray has previous experience. Gray also posted a 2.72 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, and 21.8 percent strikeout rate in 169 innings this year. Either way, the Red Sox have a nice duo set up to start the first two games of the series.

item.title: [sbnation.com] MLB Playoffs: Ranking all 12 teams by their World Series 2026 chances
