item.content:encoded:
The MLB postseason is here.
There are 12 teams headed to the playoffs including the Houston Astros and the Philadelphia Phillies, who needed wins in Game 162 to punch their respective tickets to the dance. But now, records reset to 0-0, and all 12 teams have an equal chance to win the World Series.
At least in theory.
But some teams are in a better position than others as the playoffs beckon. Here are the 12 teams in the MLB Playoffs, ranked by their chances of winning the World Series.
12. Houston Astros (81-81)
The Houston Astros became the first team in MLB history to win the division without a winning record.
This is a team that can mash, as the Astros led the majors with 226 home runs, 42 off the bat of MVP candidate Yordan Alvarez. Four other members of the lineup topped 20 home runs as well: Christian Walker, Jeremy Peña, Isaac Paredes, and Cam Smith.
But the problem is pitching, as the Astros were 24th in MLB in ERA and 21st in WHIP. Closer Josh Hader was solid in the second half, racking up 16 saves and posting a WHIP of 0.682, and Bryan Abreu has been dependable in front of him, but the bullpen has been inconsistent beyond those two.
So if the rotation cannot pitch deep into games, that will be a problem.
11. Chicago White Sox (84-78)
After losing more than 100 games in each of the past three seasons, the Chicago White Sox were one of baseball’s best stories this year, leading the AL Central for much of the season before sliding into the playoffs with a Wild Card spot.
Chicago is powered by a lineup that features three players with more than 30 home runs — Munetaka Murakami, Colson Montgomery, and Miguel Vargas — and as a team the White Sox posted an OBP 0f .320, second only to the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League.
However, the problem in the playoffs might be starting pitching. As a staff the White Sox starting pitchers posted an ERA of 4.60 this season (26th in the majors) and a WHIP of 1.34 (25th in the majors). That sets up a tough matchup, starting with the Wild Card Series against Houston.
But, they do have the Pope on their side.
10. Philadelphia Phillies (88-74)
The Philadelphia Phillies cut their magic number for a playoff spot to one with a win over the Milwaukee Brewers last Tuesday.
They lost their next four games by a combined score of 23-3, needing a win on the final day of the season to book a postseason berth.
Philadelphia did that on Sunday, clinching the final Wild Card spot in the NL with a 7-3 win over the Tampa Bay Rays, and this star-laden team now gets a series with the Atlanta Braves to prove everyone wrong. Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper, and Trae Turner bring the star power, and Jhoan Duran remains one of the best closers in baseball. Philadelphia also has Zack Wheeler and Cristopher Sánchez leading the rotation; however, manager Don Mattingly was forced to use Sánchez in the season finale, complicating his availability this week. Then there is Aaron Nola, who is coming off a spot start on short rest on Saturday and needs to play a big role despite some struggles this season.
Can a weary rotation, and a bullpen that has endured its own share of struggles in front of Duran, get the job done? That is the big question.
9. Cleveland Guardians (85-77)
While the Chicago White Sox were one of the biggest surprises of the MLB season, in the end the Cleveland Guardians clinched the AL Central, and a first-round playoff bye.
Their reward? After the bye Cleveland will have home-field advantage against the winner of the Houston-Chicago series, and they will avoid any of the AL East teams until a potential ALCS matchup.
The Guardians are led by their pitching, as Cleveland boasts both a strong rotation and a stellar bullpen. Gavin Williams and Parker Messick pace a starting staff that produced the ninth-best ERA among starters and the bullpen, led by closer Cade Smith and the trio of setup arms Hunter Gaddis, Eric Sabrowski, and Tim Herrin was even better, with the sixth-best ERA among bullpens in the majors.
If Cleveland gets enough production from the offense, that pitching staff could power them to the ALCS, where anything can happen.
8. Boston Red Sox (87-75)
After a brutal start cost manager Alex Cora his job, the Boston Red Sox used a 32-5 stretch to push into playoff contention.
But Boston cooled off after that torrid summer, and there are some questions facing this team as the playoffs loom. One is the health of the lineup. Ceddanne Rafaela is back after missing 16 games with a quad injury, but will Willson Contreras be fully healthy after getting hit by a pitch on his right hand in the final week of the season? A second question? Can the lineup bounce back after a difficult September. As a team, Boston posted an OPS of .651 in the month of September.
Pitching is not a question. The trio of Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suárez is one of the best left standing, and Aroldis Chapman has been dynamic at the back of the bullpen yet again. Boston could even get Garrett Crochet back from injury in a relief role, and Tanner Houck — who started Game 162 more than 500 days after his last MLB appearance, after working back from Tommy John surgery — could be in the mix out of the bullpen as well.
Which version of the Red Sox shows up, however, is the ultimate question.
7. Chicago Cubs (89-73)
The Chicago Cubs have one of the best offenses in baseball, led by MVP candidate Pete Crow-Armstrong, the first center fielder in MLB history to produce a 40/40 season. This is a lineup that led the majors with a team OPS of .767, and a team slugging percentage of .428. Beyond Crow-Armstrong, Alex Bregman, Ian Happ, Michael Busch, and Seiya Suzuki all put 20 home runs on the board this season.
The Cubs also have one of the best defenses in baseball, again with Crow-Armstrong leading the way. The outfielder posted a Fielding Run Value (FRV) of +26 this season, tops in the majors, and the Cubs led all teams with a FRV of +72 this year, ahead of the St. Louis Cardinals who posted a +45.
The problem? Pitching. The Cubs starters posted a team ERA of 4.27 this year — worst among NL playoff teams — and only two teams gave up more home runs than the Cubs this year. And a staff that has been hampered by injuries faces another question on that front as the playoffs loom, as Kevin Gausman was injured on a tag play last week and suffered an injury to his non-throwing shoulder. Craig Counsell would love to have him for the series against the San Diego Padres.
The Cubs have the offense and the defense to win games, but do they have the pitching to win a series or two?
6. San Diego Padres (91-71)
If momentum could be measured, the San Diego Padres might be off the charts.
The Padres went 17-11 in August, and then 18-6 in September, to lock down a Wild Card spot. This was quite the turnaround for a team that was flirting with being sellers at the trade deadline. Leading the way was outfielder Fernando Tatis Jr., who did not homer over the first 55 games of the season but finished with 25 home runs and 38 steals, thanks to a torrid closing stretch. Jackson Merrill overcame a slow start of his own to finish with 26 home runs and 27 steals, giving the Padres their first 25/25 duo.
As a lineup, the Padres were second in both OPS and slugging percentage after the All-Star break, behind only the Cubs.
San Diego also has one of the best bullpens in baseball, with closer Mason Miller in form behind setup men Adrian Morejon and Bradgley Rodriguez.
They’ll host the Cubs in the Wild Card Series, and while Chicago won the season series 5-1, that was before San Diego’s late-season turnaround.
5. New York Yankees (93-68)
When the New York Yankees lost Aaron Judge for an extended period of the regular season, the lineup stepped up in his absence. While Judge played just 66 games and hit 18 home runs, the Yankees managed to belt 223 home runs, finishing second in the majors.
But with his status in question for the Wild Card Series against Boston, the rest of that lineup will need to step up yet again. And the matchup against the Red Sox will be a tough one, as Boston will likely throw Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suárez against them — a strong start — and the Red Sox have one of the best bullpens in the game.
And that matchup will be even tougher without Judge’s bat in the lineup.
4. Atlanta Braves (94-67)
While the Atlanta Braves would have loved a first-round bye, with the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Milwaukee Brewers out of striking distance Atlanta was able to set their rotation for the Wild Card Series over the final week of the season. Chris Sale made his final start of the regular season last Wednesday on extra rest, and will be on extra rest when he gets the ball for Game 1. The same goes for Tyler Mahle, who will have extra rest ahead of an anticipated Game 2 start.
Plus the Braves get the Philadelphia Phillies in the Wild Card Series, who gave their fans something to worry about over the final few days of the season as they did not clinch a spot until Game 162.
3. Tampa Bay Rays (98-64)
Few people gave the Tampa Bay Rays a chance when the season began.
Leading with me, who put the Rays in the “True Longshots” category when the year began, along with the Diamondbacks, the Athletics, and the Twins.
But here are the Rays, the winners of the AL East and the team to beat in the American League. MCP candidate Junior Caminero has put up massive numbers for Tampa Bay — he slashed .276/.360/.524 this year along with 42 home runs — and is at the heart of a lineup that punishes pitchers from top-to-bottom. As a team the Rays hit .258 this season, the best number in the AL and tied with the Brewers for the top number in the majors, and the Rays also posted a team OPS of .728, behind only the Houston Astros in the American League.
Add in a staff that posted an MLB-best team WHIP of 1.14, tied with the Dodgers, and you have the recipe for a deep playoff run.
2. Los Angeles Dodgers (100-62)
The Los Angeles Dodgers got off to their annual hot start, endured a mid-season slump that raised more questions than answers about their chances at a three-peat, but enter the playoffs having found some of those answers.
Kyle Tucker’s season-long slump seems to be ending just in time for a post-season run, as he slashed .266/362/.557 in the month of September, his best stretch of the season by far. Shohei Ohtani and Will Smith are both back in the lineup, Edwin Diaz seems to have found his stuff — he was flawless in September, allowing just one hit in four appearances and striking out eight — and Mookie Betts is back to being Mookie Betts, as he slashed .345/.447/.690 in September, also putting up his best numbers of the season.
When you’ve won a pair of titles, you know when to turn it on.
The Dodgers seem to have done just that over the last month.
1. Milwaukee Brewers (103-59)
The Milwaukee Brewers top these rankings, as they topped 100 wins for the first time in franchise history.
But for this team, the real test comes in October. The Brewers have now won the NL Central for four consecutive years, and in five of the last six campaigns. What do they have to show for that? Two playoff wins, including a sweep at the hands of the Dodgers in the NLCS a year ago.
Jacob Misiorowski gives them a bonafide ace, as the big right-hander led the majors in ERA (1.86), ERA+ (225), WHIP (0.803), and K/9 (13.1) this season, and Logan Henderson has developed into a solid No. 2 for Milwaukee. If Kyle Harrison somehow recovers his first-half form (he was 8-2 with a 3.01 ERA before the All-Star Break, but went 3-3 with a 7.31 ERA in the second half of the season) this team could finally break through to the promised land.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox Get Timely Brayan Bello Boost Ahead of Wild Card Series
item.dc:creator: Keith Watkins
item.description: The Boston Red Sox needed pitching in Game 2 of Friday's doubleheader against the Chicago Cubs. Brayan Bello gave them four shutout innings. When he walked off the mound for the last time in the regular season, the Fenway crowd rose. Bello got a standing ovation. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox needed pitching in Game 2 of Friday's doubleheader against the Chicago Cubs. Brayan Bello gave them four shutout innings.
When he walked off the mound for the last time in the regular season, the Fenway crowd rose. Bello got a standing ovation.
Five months ago, he was pitching in Worcester after being optioned out of the big-league rotation. Friday's ovation told the story of how far he has come since.
From Worcester to Red Sox Weapon
Bello's 2026 started as badly as any season can. He posted a 10.35 ERA across eight starts before the Red Sox sent him to Triple-A in late April. Something needed to change.
What changed was the role. Bello came back as a bulk reliever and the transformation was immediate. The fastball carried more life. The command sharpened. The confidence returned.
Since rejoining the big-league staff, Bello has posted a 2.28 ERA and a 1.01 WHIP over his last 51.1 innings across 13 appearances. The Red Sox eventually gave him starts again, and he responded with his best stretch of the season.
Over his last four outings spanning 18⅔ innings, Bello has allowed just one earned run. That translates to a 0.48 ERA heading into October.
What Friday Showed
Bello's performance capped a September that has erased any remaining questions about his role in the postseason. His 11-strikeout outing against the Athletics on September 19 was the exclamation point on a second half that turned his entire season around.
The standing ovation from the Fenway crowd carried weight because of everything that preceded it. This was not a player who cruised through the year. This was someone who got sent down, rebuilt his approach, and fought his way back into being one of the most trusted arms on the staff.
"I learned not to let bad moments dictate how the next one is going to be," Bello said.
Where Bello Fits in October
The Red Sox will likely use Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez as their three starters in the Wild Card Series against the New York Yankees. That leaves Bello available out of the bullpen, where he has been at his best.
His ability to provide multiple innings of high-quality relief makes him a critical piece in a best-of-three format. If a starter runs into trouble early or the Red Sox need to bridge a gap between a short outing and the back end of the bullpen, Bello is the arm built for that moment.
The Red Sox invested in Bello believing in his ceiling. The second half of 2026 is the closest he has come to reaching it.
Final Word for the Red Sox
Brayan Bello got sent to the minors in April. He came back a different pitcher. The numbers since his return tell that story clearly, but the standing ovation at Fenway told it better.
The postseason starts Tuesday. Bello enters it on the best run of his career, with a 0.48 ERA over his last four outings and the confidence of a team that knows exactly what he can provide.
Five months ago, he was in Worcester. Friday night, the Fenway crowd was on its feet for him. That is the kind of arc that carries into October.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Red Sox Get Timely Brayan Bello Boost Ahead of Wild Card Series appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Pedro Martinez defends Blue Jays star after contract remark controversy
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: Thursday night Pedro Martinez stopped by Fenway Park, and while making the rounds the Red Sox legend held court in the back of the press box to talk about the team, his day working with elementary school students in Lawrence earlier in the afternoon, and the upcoming Red Sox-Yankees playoff rematch. But before wrapping up, he addressed one other matter close to his heart. Toronto Blue Jays slugger Vladimir Guerrero Jr., whose Hall of Fame father played with Martinez with the Montreal Expos and w
item.content:encoded:
Thursday night Pedro Martinez stopped by Fenway Park, and while making the rounds the Red Sox legend held court in the back of the press box to talk about the team, his day working with elementary school students in Lawrence earlier in the afternoon, and the upcoming Red Sox-Yankees playoff rematch.
But before wrapping up, he addressed one other matter close to his heart.
Toronto Blue Jays slugger Vladimir Guerrero Jr., whose Hall of Fame father played with Martinez with the Montreal Expos and was a fellow Dominican Republic great, recently raised eyebrows when he made comments in a Spanish-language interview suggesting that his 14-year, $500 million contract was a reward for past performance and not an investment by the Blue Jays into his future potential.
“I want people to understand one thing,” Guerrero said in Spanish, per MLB.com’s translation. “The money they gave me wasn’t for what I’m going to do. It was for what I already did. They didn’t pay me because I’m going to hit 40 every year. They paid me for what I already accomplished. People are confused about that, but I think the same way they do. Like, sometimes I even say to myself: bro, they gave you all that money and you’re out here doing nothing. I try.”
Those remarks drew criticism from Blue Jays fans and from across the sport, but Martinez, who is Guerrero’s godfather, said he believes his comments were widely misinterpreted.
“What he meant was he’s got a contract probably because of the things he did and what he might do in the future,” Martinez said. “That’s a young man talking that didn’t really explain himself, he got paid based on what he did and what he might do in the future, it’s a projection.”
While Guerrero initially stood by his comments when asked on Wednesday, he addressed the matter again on Friday and apologized to fans for the impression he’d given. He said he’d also spoken to Blue Jays manager John Schneider and apologized to his teammates for the distraction the whole ordeal had caused.
“I just gave it some thought, and I felt like the comments I made the other day were not really what I wanted to say,” Guerrero said, per Keegan Matheson of MLB.com. “I felt that everyone, my fans and everyone, deserves an apology from me.”
The firestorm comes amid a disappointing season for Guerrero, who is already a six-time All-Star at age 27 and helped lead the Blue Jays to within inches of a World Series championship last fall. But after averaging nearly 32 home runs per year over his last five seasons, Guerrero has hit only nine homers this year to go along with a massive drop in production across the board.
The Blue Jays, initially a favorite to repeat as American League champions, missed the playoffs and will finish with a losing record.
Schneider stood up for Guerrero as a teammate and a leader, and Martinez, who has known Guerrero since he was a young boy, vouched for his character, insisting that he isn’t the type of person who’d rest on his laurels.
“Vlad is not that arrogant guy that’s going to be saying ‘ahh I got paid and that’s it and I’m going to sit down,’ no, Vlady’s a gamer! We all know it,” Martinez said. “So don’t let those people that want to really ruin a good player get to that point.”
Pedro on Tracy, Breslow
Among his comments Thursday, Martinez also offered high praise for Red Sox manager Chad Tracy and chief baseball officer Craig Breslow, who both recently received long-term job security that will keep them leading the organization through the end of the decade.
Tracy, the Hall of Famer said, has done a great job pressing all the right buttons and getting the most out of his young players.
“Outstanding. Outstanding. You couldn’t ask for more. If you asked for more you’re being greedy,” Martinez said. “This is a guy that quietly, under the table, has done what he needs to do, not that Alex (Cora) didn’t do it because we saw Alex do an outstanding job, but the young team that we have has somehow clicked with him.”
Martinez also was a fan of the moves Breslow made at the trade deadline to help bolster the club’s roster ahead of the playoff push.
“Breslow deserves a lot of credit for the movement he made during the deadline, for how everything is working, for the entire team and the organization,” Martinez said. “We have to give to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and so far the job has been done right.”
Big fan of Tolle
Since debuting for the Red Sox late in the 2025 season, Payton Tolle has endeared himself to Red Sox fans through both his dominant performances on the mound and his larger-than-life personality.
He’s won over Martinez too, who said he loves how Tolle pitches with such infectious energy and wishes he could have learned to embrace that kind of attitude during his playing days.
“I wish I could teach myself at an early age how to be like Tolle,” Martinez said. “The guy laughs, the guy pitches, the guy is a bully, the guy is big and intimidating, he’s got everything.”
Martinez said he appreciates guys like Tolle and New York Mets reliever Jefry Yan — who often performs a dramatic jumping celebration after each strikeout — for what they bring to the game. Martinez was famously as no nonsense as you could possibly be during his playing career, but despite their apparent differences Martinez also appreciates the edge Tolle pitches with as well.
“At the same time he’s out there to beat you,” Martinez said. “He’s a bully. I love him, I love him, and he’s aware of everything he’s doing, even though he’s laughing and goofing around, you see him graciously, I think he’s doing what he needs to do and even more, having fun with it, something I couldn’t do.”

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Red Sox hoping investment in Ranger Suarez pays off again in the postseason - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Peter Abraham

item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox made their biggest investment of the offseason in January when they signed free agent lefthander Ranger Suarez for five years and $130 million.
Eight months later, it’s fair to say Suarez did what was expected.
He was 8-5 with a 3.22 earned run average over 28 starts and 148 innings. Suarez was an All-Star, and the Sox were 17-11 in the games he started. Outside of missing three starts with a groin strain and a sore lower back, Suarez was a reliable rotation pillar.
He allowed one earned run or none in 16 starts. That’s right in line with how he pitched for the Phillies in 2024 and ’25.
Suarez allowed one run on three hits over five innings in a 1-0 loss against the Guardians on Thursday night. The one run came on a 319-foot Pesky Pole home run by Angel Martinez in the second inning.
Otherwise, Suarez stayed in control despite throwing 39 pitches over the first two innings.
“When you look at the body of work, especially coupled with the other guys in the rotation, he was fantastic,” manager Chad Tracy said. “He had a great year.”
Suarez wasn’t quite so complimentary of himself.
“In general, good,” he said via a translator. “Obviously I think I could have done better. But I was happy I was able to finish the season strong.”
Now comes the true test.
Suarez was 4-1 with a 1.48 ERA in 11 postseason games for the Phillies, eight of them as a starter. Philadelphia won eight of those games.
That includes Game 3 of the Division Series against the Dodgers last season when Suarez pitched five innings out of the bullpen and held the mighty Dodgers to one run at Dodger Stadium. That’s what he’s capable of in a big game.
Suarez is likely to start Game 3 in the Wild Card Series next week, which means he could have a huge say in whether this memorable season will continue.
“Being able to finish this month strong, I think, is going to be the key for the playoffs,” Suarez said.
Suarez was referring to the 1.09 ERA and 0.93 WHIP he posted over his final four starts.
His results against the Yankees this season were less encouraging. Suarez faced them three times and allowed 11 earned runs over 16 innings.
But he did have a strong start at Yankee Stadium on June 7, allowing one run over 6 innings against Cam Schlittler. It was 1-1 when Suarez left the game; then the bullpen allowed five runs.
Tracy has not revealed his rotation for the series. But if he stays in order, it would be Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Suarez.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone has held back that information, too.
Schlittler, who is a heavy favorite to win the Cy Young Award, would make sense to start Game 1. He dominated the Sox in four starts this season, allowing two earned runs over 24 innings and striking out 27.
A Tolle-Schlittler matchup would be must-viewing for even a casual baseball fan.
But there is speculation that the Yankees would save Schlittler for Game 2 and give Game 1 to lefthander Max Fried, who also has pitched well against the Sox this season.
That might be overthinking it, but it’s an option.
Based on the last few games, the Red Sox will need their pitchers to be close to perfect. Tracy has used the last 10 days to give his regulars rest while giving extra time off to players who have been dealing with injuries.
The Sox have scored only five runs over their last five games and hit .222. Willson Contreras, who was thought to be progressing well from a bruised right hand, said after the game he was concerned about being ready for the Yankees series.
“I’m doing everything that I can to come back and play with the boys and be with them,” Suarez said. “But sometimes you have to listen to your body.”
If Contreras can’t play, or is compromised, that would put even more pressure on the pitchers.
“This team can pitch,” Suarez said. “We’ll be ready for next week.”
Peter Abraham can be reached at peter.abraham@globe.com. Follow him on Bluesky at peteabeglobe.bsky.social.

item.title: [NBC Boston] Red Sox legend Pedro Martinez launches coding program for kids in Lawrence
item.dc:creator: Malcolm Johnson
item.description: When Pedro Martinez was on the mound for the Boston Red Sox, he was a fan favorite. More than 20 years later, as schoolchildren cheered and swarmed around him for autographs Thursday in Lawrence, Massachusetts, it was clear that has not changed. The baseball Hall of Famer's childhood struggles continue to inspire his commitment to giving back. Martinez and his wife, Carolina, are launching a new afterschool coding program serving seven elementary schools in Lawrence. "I had to struggle for every
item.content:encoded:
When Pedro Martinez was on the mound for the Boston Red Sox, he was a fan favorite.
More than 20 years later, as schoolchildren cheered and swarmed around him for autographs Thursday in Lawrence, Massachusetts, it was clear that has not changed.
The baseball Hall of Famer's childhood struggles continue to inspire his commitment to giving back. Martinez and his wife, Carolina, are launching a new afterschool coding program serving seven elementary schools in Lawrence.
"I had to struggle for everything I achieved in life, and I just want to make it easier for others to get to where I got," Martinez said.
The program will give hundreds of third- and fourth-grade students access to modern technology and opportunities to develop coding and problem-solving skills.
"Maybe because it's something I was denied when I was younger," Martinez said when asked why the program is so important to him.
Martinez spoke with students at Lawrence schools as part of a back-to-school celebration, where children also received school supplies and gift bags.
The program is focused on reaching students early, Carolina Martinez said.
"Their age mattered to us in terms of the decision, because the earlier you get them, the more motivated they're going to be, but also, the more resourceful they're going to be later on," she said.
South Lawrence East Elementary School Principal Lori Butterfield said students are already immersed in technology, and the program will help them move from simply using technology to creating with it.
"They love playing games. They love using apps. They're using AI all the time. I want them to learn how to create those things, and I think this program will allow them to do that," Butterfield said.
For Martinez, the connection to Lawrence is personal.
"Why? Because in Lawrence, I quickly identified the need, I found my culture, I found my people here. I found my roots," he said.
Martinez also reflected on what can happen when young people are given even one opportunity.
"Remember, what you're seeing right now is the product of an opportunity. Only one, and that's all it took," he said.
Martinez seized his own opportunities on the mound, becoming one of baseball's most accomplished pitchers.
With the Red Sox preparing to face the Yankees in the postseason, Martinez was asked how he would feel about taking the mound today.
"I'll be ready from here, to give them all the knowledge and everything, all the experience I've done before — I'm ready to do that any day," he said. "But physically, to go pitch? I have Payton Tolle and I have Sonny Gray to go do it for me."
Martinez said he plans to continue coming back to Lawrence and contributing to the community — a place he now considers home.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Red Sox try Patrick Sandoval out of bullpen but bats go quiet as Guardians clinch playoff spot - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Tim Healey
item.description: In these waning days of the regular season, the Red Sox are trying something new: Patrick Sandoval, reliever. Sandoval tossed a scoreless sixth inning in a 1-0 loss to the Guardians on Thursday, his first appearance out of the bullpen since 2021. item.content:encoded:
In these waning days of the regular season, the Red Sox are trying something new: Patrick Sandoval, reliever.
Sandoval tossed a scoreless sixth inning in a 1-0 loss to the Guardians on Thursday, his first appearance out of the bullpen since 2021.
It was a successfully uneventful frame at Fenway Park: After José Ramírez grounded a single through the left side of the infield and stole second, Sandoval retired Chase DeLauter (strikeout looking), Jo Adell (ground out), and Angel Martínez (ground out). His velocity was down a tad in the small sample size of 12 pitches (10 strikes), but he was pitching just three days after his most recent start.
Ahead of the playoffs opening Tuesday, the Sandoval twist is of particular note because of his recent struggles as a starter and the Red Sox’ recent struggles looking for a reliable lefthanded reliever.
As a member of the rotation, Sandoval had a 5.15 ERA in 13 outings this year. That included a 7.32 mark in four starts this month. He has appeared unlikely to fit into the postseason plans in that role.
Also of late, Erik Miller, the team’s top lefty reliever, has had a bad time, entering the day with a 8.53 ERA in seven appearances this month. Of the 36 hitters he had faced, 17 had reached base: six hits, a whopping nine walks, and two batters hit by pitches.
Immediately after Sandoval departed, though, Miller entered — and maybe figured it out. He turned in a perfect seventh on just eight pitches, getting a strikeout of David Fry, a routine fly out from Travis Bazzana, and a 108-miles-per-hour line out from Patrick Bailey.
The loss dropped the Red Sox to 85-74 and — with three games to go — ensured that they will not match their 89 wins from last year.
They totaled two hits. Nick Sogard and Jarren Duran each had a single. It was the fourth game this month in which the Sox recorded four hits or fewer.
Lefthander Ranger Suarez finished a strong September — and strong regular season — with five innings of one-run ball. He held the Guardians to three hits and a walk and struck out five.
Cleveland’s lone run against him came on Martínez’s home run, tucked inside the Pesky Pole, an estimated 319 feet down the right-field line. It came off his bat at only 94 m.p.h. The batted ball had an expected batting average of .160.
At the end of the first season of a five-year, $130 million contract, Suarez owns a 3.22 ERA, third best in the Red Sox’ rotation behind righthander Sonny Gray (2.72) and lefthander Payton Tolle (3.03).
Suarez suffered from a midseason dip — a groin injury followed by mediocrity — but rebounded late, posting a 1.09 ERA over his final four starts.
The Sox mustered minimal offense against opener Daniel Espino (perfect first inning with two strikeouts) and lefthander Joey Cantillo (one hit and no runs in five innings).
For Cantillo, who entered the night with the most walks in the American League (79) but issued just two free passes against the Red Sox, it was his third consecutive scoreless appearance. In all three, he entered behind an opener.
Tim Healey can be reached at timothy.healey@globe.com. Follow him @timbhealey.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Pedro Martinez on Game 7 in 2003, no regrets on calling the Yankees his daddy, and a mission to help - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Dan Shaughnessy
item.description: Many of us believe he’s the best pitcher we’ve ever seen. item.content:encoded:
Many of us believe he’s the best pitcher we’ve ever seen. He’s a blue-chip, first-ballot Hall of Famer, part of the Red Sox team that broke the Curse, and seen on TBS after Sox playoff games in any given October. He’ll be 55 next month and spends every year shuttling between Boston and his native Dominican Republic, when he’s not working in Atlanta. He has no regrets about saying “The Yankees are my daddy,” all those years ago, and he thinks the Red Sox have a shot to beat the Yankees in New York next week.
He is the one and only Pedro Martinez, and he’s spending Thursday in Lawrence with his wife, Carolina, launching an after-school coding program at South Lawrence East Elementary School, then engaging in a question-and-answer session with hundreds of students at Lawrence High School.
“Lawrence has been kind of forgotten a little bit,” said Martinez. “It has gotten kind of old in front of our eyes, but there is so much need. If there’s something I can really identify myself with, it is need. I grew up in those kind of needs. I’m just expressing the cry I had when I was a kid. I get excited every time I see a kid that has an opportunity to become someone.”
Martinez’s new program is designed to bridge resource gaps and enhance classroom learning for young students across Lawrence. His foundation, dedicated to transforming the lives of youth in the United States and the Dominican Republic, was started in 1998 when he joined the Sox after five-plus stellar seasons with the Dodgers and Expos.
“I got a very pleasant surprise when I got to Fenway as soon as I saw the drums and the people with the [Dominican] flag and the atmosphere kind of changing,” Martinez recalled. “Mayor [Thomas] Menino was kind enough to take me in his SUV to give me a tour around Boston, and right away I fell in love with the people … and the Latino community all over the place, and that’s when I landed in Lawrence, Lynn, Dorchester, and all those areas that continue to be linked to me.”
It was in those early Boston days that Martinez’s Fenway mound starts “became the curfew back home in the Dominican every time I pitched.”
A connection was made; an ongoing, lasting relationship because of the Pedro Martinez Foundation.
In 2026, Martinez and teammate/countryman David Ortiz are listed as “special assistants” in the fourth line of the the Red Sox’ official front office directory, just below chief baseball officer Craig Breslow. Martinez occasionally helps young Sox pitchers at spring training, but he was out of the loop when the decision was made to fire manager Alex Cora and six coaches just 27 games into the season.
“I was actually talking to Alex a couple of days before,” Martinez remembered. “When I found out, I wasn’t angry, I just couldn’t understand how everything snowballed to that point.”
Martinez’s beloved former teammate, catcher/captain Jason Varitek, was part of the purge. The Sox claimed Varitek was “reassigned,” but he hasn’t surfaced anywhere in the organization.
Does Martinez think the burned bridge will be repaired?
“I think it’s going to be OK with Jason,” said the three-time Cy Young Award winner. “Jason is a very professional person. He understands that business part, just like Alex Cora.”
What does Martinez think about the local demonization of Rafael Devers?
“This is a very misunderstood kid,” he said. “Devers is very shy. But he is legit. He’s a guy that doesn’t know how to express himself and has a hard time trusting anybody but his father. His father knows the actual truth … Devers is very respectful, a very lovely kid, but now it’s over and the team is on its way to success. … You have to learn to love Boston if you want to survive in Boston. Boston is 24/7 talking about their sports.”
Does Martinez want Payton Tolle or Sonny Gray starting Game 1?
“You don’t go wrong with either one,” he said. “Sonny is a true professional, a true competitor. I love, love Tolle. Just his amazing attitude. I love every single pitch he throws. I love everything about him.
“The Yankees are vulnerable, especially without [Aaron] Judge. I don’t think the Red Sox are intimidated by the Yankees. I think they can beat not only the Yankees but any team in baseball.”
The highlight of Martinez’s baseball career?
“Being part of the 25 that brought the trophy to Boston.”
Ever wish he never said, “The Yankees are my daddy”?
“No. I was being honest. That’s what you guys demand from all of us. The Yankees had my number at that point, and I expressed it. I will tell you in the most honest way, I got my ass kicked.”
Which brings us back to 2003, when Grady Little was fired (almost immediately) after failing to take Martinez out of the game when Pedro was past his pitch limit after seven innings of Game 7 of the ALCS at Yankee Stadium. Martinez had fanned Alfonso Soriano on his final pitch of the seventh, was at 100 pitches, and believed he was done for the night.
“[Red Sox pitching coach] Dave Wallace told me I was done after, so I didn’t put my jacket on,” said Martinez. “I had looked up in the sky and gave thanks to God for the seven innings I pitched. Our bullpen was lights out. All of a sudden Grady was like, ‘I don’t like [Alan] Embree against Nick Johnson in the eighth.’ He said, ‘You give me Nick Johnson and I got the rest of the bullpen for you.’ That’s the true story.”
Back on the mound, leading, 5-2, in the eighth, Martinez retired Johnson on a second-pitch popup to start the inning, then looked to the dugout. Nobody moved.
“Nothing happened,” recalled Martinez. “So I just kept going. I gave up a couple of line drives, and everything just snowballed after that. I thought I made a great pitch on [Jorge] Posada, but Posada blooped it [for a two-run double].”
All in all, it was four straight hits and a tie game before Little finally pulled Martinez after 23 disastrous eighth-inning pitches. Then Aaron Boone (now the Yankees’ manager) happened in the 11th.
Two summers ago, Maryland congressman Jamie Raskin wrote President Joe Biden a letter, imploring America’s tiring leader to end his reelection campaign. As part of his logic, Raskin compared Biden’s career to Martinez’s Game 7 performance, writing that there is “no shame in taking a well-deserved bow … when your arm is tired out.”
Days later, Biden pulled out of the race.
“I don’t know what to tell you about that,” chuckled Martinez. “Grady just told me, ‘Get one more out.’ That was Nick Johnson, right?”
Right.
All these years later, the wounds have healed and Martinez is on a greater mission, taking his message to Lawrence.
“I don’t have enough words to describe how grateful I am to have my opportunity through baseball and make a difference now,” said Martinez. “My message to these kids in Lawrence is that nothing in life is too far away if you have the will, if you have the passion.”
Dan Shaughnessy is a Globe columnist. He can be reached at daniel.shaughnessy@globe.com. Follow him @dan_shaughnessy.

item.title: [blogs.fangraphs.com] The Weakest Positions on the Remaining American League Contenders
item.dc:creator: Jay Jaffe

item.content:encoded:
The Yankees had to make do without Aaron Judge for all of June, July and August due to a stress fracture in his right first rib. With the days on the calendar dwindling and the AL East title still in play — which is no longer the case after the Rays clinched on Tuesday night — Judge bypassed a rehab assignment, but once he returned, he played in just seven games before landing back on the injured list due to a right calf strain. Both the slugger and the team took great pains to avoid discussing the injury’s specificity and timeline for recovery until Tuesday, when manager Aaron Boone revealed that Judge has a “moderate grade” strain, received a platelet-poor plasma injection, and isn’t expected to be available for the team’s Wild Card Series rematch against the Red Sox.
While deadline acquisition Heliot Ramos has heated up after a very slow start to his pinstriped career, the Yankees’ right field situation is one of the more glaring potential trouble spots among American League contenders. As the playoffs approach, teams no longer have a chance to upgrade from outside their organizations and instead must make do with the talent on hand. What follows here is a look at the most vulnerable teams at each position — something of a companion to my annual pre-deadline Replacement Level Killers series, with a focus on the teams that still have a chance to make the playoffs. For the AL, that means the Rays, Yankees, and Red Sox — all of whom have clinched spots — plus the Guardians, White Sox, Rangers, and Astros, who are battling for the other two division titles and the third Wild Card spot. I’ve taken the Blue Jays out of consideration, as their Playoff Odds now start with a zero in front of the decimal. While full-season performances play a significant part here, I’m more concerned with who’s worst now, with injuries and adjustments in mind. Each position has a headliner (or two, if it’s a job share), but at several positions, I’ve noted other teams with concerns. A companion National League piece will follow.
Catcher: Kyle Teel and Jake Rogers, White Sox
A Top 100 prospect in both 2024 and ’25, Kyle Teel did a very solid job as a rookie last season, hitting for a 125 wRC+ with 1.9 WAR in just 78 games, but he missed the first two months of this season due to a Grade 2 right hamstring strain and then an LCL sprain in his right knee. His replacements, mainly Edgar Quero (a three-time Top 100 prospect) and Drew Romo, struggled so mightily that they headed the catchers’ section on my Replacement Level Killers list, with Quero optioned to Triple-A Charlotte once Teel returned. While Teel’s defense has been an upgrade, he’s hit just .178/.302/.318 (81 wRC+) with an astronomical 37.3% strikeout rate, up from last year’s 25.9%, and his average exit velocity is just 84.5 mph, down from last year’s 88.3 mph. He recently missed time with a left ankle sprain as well.
Romo was optioned to Charlotte in early September during a shuffle that included both Teel’s return and the arrival of the 31-year-old Jake Rogers via the waiver wire. Rogers, who began the year with the Tigers, was traded to the Orioles in late July, then flipped to the Red Sox in the Adley Rutschman trade on August 3 before being sent on his merry way again within a fortnight. He’s now playing for his fourth team this season and has hit just .161/.276/.287 (62 wRC+). All told, White Sox catchers have combined for a 54 wRC+ and -0.4 WAR, both of which rank 29th in the majors; for as much long-term potential as the 24-year-old Teel and 23-year-old Quero (who has played sparingly since being recalled) may have, they’re less than ideal right now.
It’s worth noting that Rutschman, who was on the injured list due to left wrist inflammation when he was sent to Boston as part of a seven-player blockbuster, has struggled to the point that he’s a concern as well. The 28-year-old switch-hitter was batting a solid .251/.331/.433 (116 wRC+) before being sidelined for three weeks — his third IL stint this season, with shorter ones for left ankle inflammation and a concussion while with Baltimore — but he’s hit just .214/.270/.398 (82 wRC+) in 111 plate appearances since being activated. His strikeout rate has spiked from 14.1% to 21.6%, and his average exit velo has fallen by about two ticks. Backup Connor Wong has hit a similarly light .234/.310/.346 (84 wRC+), albeit with dreadful defense (-10 FRV, -8 DRS, -6.6 FRM). The good news is that Rutschman went 3-for-4 with a pair of doubles on Tuesday night against the Guardians; the bad news is that the Red Sox have other injury concerns in their lineup as well.
First Base: Nathaniel Lowe and David Fry, Guardians
Guardians first basemen made my Killers list due to the light production of their platoon of Kyle Manzardo and Rhys Hoskins. At the deadline, they dealt for Nathaniel Lowe and optioned Manzardo to Triple-A Columbus. A couple of week later, they placed Hoskins on the IL due to lower back inflammation and turned to David Fry, a utilityman who can catch. Alas, after getting a 94 wRC+ from their first basemen prior to the deadline, they’ve managed just a 90 wRC+ since. The lefty-swinging Lowe, who hit a robust .266/.341/.480 (123 wRC+) for the Reds, has dipped to .228/.279/.390 (83 wRC+) while hitting a ton of popups. The righty-swinging Fry has done well in his limited duty at first base, but has hit just .192/.312/.349 (90 wRC+) in 202 plate appearances overall.
Hoskins began a swing progression nearly two weeks ago, but with Columbus’ season having ended, a rehab assignment isn’t an option, which doesn’t bode well for an uptick from his .179/.306/.376 (95 wRC+) line. Manzardo (.215/.306/.378, 95 wRC+) didn’t hit the ball as hard at Columbus as he had either in his previous stops there or in Cleveland, and there hasn’t been any buzz about bringing him back in September or October.
Meanwhile in Boston, Willson Contreras has been the team’s top hitter, batting a potent .276/.387/.518 (152 wRC+) with 27 homers, but he’s been limited to four games this month between a left hamstring strain and a hit-by-pitch induced bruised knuckle on his right hand. Fortunately, he avoided a fracture, and returned to swinging a bat on September 20; the Red Sox hope to get him into the lineup before the end of the regular season, but the situation bears monitoring. Mickey Gasper and Nick Sogard have shared duties during his absence. Both have provided above-average production overall; Gasper had been in a 4-for-32 slump before hitting a pinch-homer — his 10th long ball in 218 plate appearances — against the Guardians on Tuesday night.
Second Base: Jose Altuve, Astros
Jose Altuve may wind up in Cooperstown some day, but Father Time has caught up to the diminutive 36-year-old. He’s batting just .250/.308/.402, which has taken a bite out of both the Astros’ offense and his chances at reaching 3,000 hits; his 99 wRC+ is his lowest full-season mark since 2013, while his .327 xSLG is a 57-point drop from last season and a Statcast-era low. What’s more, his defense has reached its nadir, with both his -10 FRV and -16 DRS rating not only as career worsts but also major league worsts at his position. With Yordan Alvarez entrenched at designated hitter and too valuable to risk in left field — he hasn’t used his glove in a postseason game since 2023 — there’s no place to hide Altuve, but also little likelihood he’ll be benched in favor of backup Nick Allen (.271/.318/.371, 95 wRC+).
On the injury front, keep an eye on the return of the Yankees’ Jazz Chisholm Jr., who was activated between games of Tuesday’s doubleheader against the Rays after missing 12 games due to a sprained right thumb. While his offense has dipped from a 125 wRC+ last year to 100 (.233/.313/.403) this year, Chisholm’s 3.4 WAR ranks third among the team’s position players behind Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger, and his total of 19 home runs ranks second. Backups Anthony Volpe (.244/.321/.335, 88 wRC+) and José Caballero (.236/.293/.373, 86 wRC+) are substantial steps down, but if Chisholm has any lingering issues, one of them may be needed to fill in.
Third Base: Ryan McMahon and Amed Rosario, Yankees
Yankees third basemen have combined for -0.1 WAR, the majors’ third-lowest mark. Lefty-swinging Ryan McMahon bears the bulk of the responsibility for that, hitting just .206/.274/.341 (73 wRC+) while playing solid defense. Righty-swinging Amed Rosario has produced a 100 wRC+ while playing third but has hit just .233/.275/.406 (87 wRC+) overall, and he’s been lousy at the hot corner, with -6 DRS and -6 FRV in just 309.1 innings. The righty-swinging Caballero is at least a better defender than Rosario and about on par offensively, and he’s one of the league’s top base thieves, with 34 steals in 45 attempts. He has also out-produced Rosario against lefties, with an 81 wRC+ to Rosario’s 63 — which could be a factor given that the Red Sox can call upon lefties Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle to start during the Wild Card Series.
Shortstop: Taylor Walls, Rays
For the third year in a row, the defensive metrics have been very split with regards to Taylor Walls. His 21 DRS leads all shortstops (nobody else has more than 10 DRS), but his -2 FRV ranks 23rd out of 30 with at least 500 innings at the position. Between the latter mark and his dismal .222/.308/.294 (73 wRC+) line, he’s produced just 0.7 WAR. That said, neither Jorge Mateo (.205/.250/.318, 55 wRC+) nor Ben Williamson (.244/.304/.327, 79 wRC+), his occasional fill-ins, hits well enough to merit surpassing Wells on the depth chart.
Left Field: Taylor Trammell and LaMonte Wade Jr., Astros
The Astros’ current 1.3 WAR from their left fielders ranks 17th in the majors, ahead of both the Guardians (1.2) and Red Sox (0.8). But between Steven Kwan’s second-half heater and Roman Anthony’s return from a torn tendon in his right ring finger, both of those teams are now in a better spot than Houston. Taylor Trammell made several Top 100 lists as a prospect — he was as high as no. 12 as a 60-FV on our 2019 list — but he’s now 29 and has netted 0.1 WAR in 273 major league games for four different teams. This year he’s hit .200/.292/.355 (84 wRC+) in a career-high 95 games spread across the three outfield positions, with a 95 wRC+ in 237 plate appearances against righties and a 19 wRC+ (ouch) in 41 plate appearances against lefties.
LaMonte Wade Jr., a reliable contributor for the Giants from 2021–24, bottomed out to a 53 wRC+ last year in a season split between San Francisco and Anaheim. He spent the first few months of this season in the White Sox organization but was released on June 1 so he could sign with the Astros, for whom he’s hit .208/.308/.352 (90 wRC+). He’s been protected from facing many lefties and has seen his playing time dry up otherwise, as he’s been in a slump since mid-August. Meanwhile, righty-swinging Nelson Velázquez hasn’t made a very strong case for himself by hitting .192/.255/.414 (81 wRC+) with a 33.6% strikeout rate in 110 plate appearances split between the Cardinals and Astros. With options like these, you can see why playing Alvarez in left and DHing Altuve starts to make some sense.
Center Field: Daulton Varsho, Astros
The first-half struggles of Jake Meyers, Brice Matthews and Trammell landed the Astros on the Killers center field list, so they quite reasonably dealt for Daulton Varsho on August 3. The 30-year-old flychaser was hitting .243/.307/.375 (91 wRC+), and while his once-elite defense has regressed towards average, a performance like that is still good enough to carry the position. He looked like a decent upgrade for Houston, but while his defense has remained solid enough, he’s hit an anemic .172/.224/.311 (48 wRC+), with his strikeout and walk rates both moving in the wrong direction.
A closer look shows that Varsho has actually been hitting the ball slightly harder since the trade, but all season, he’s been producing popups and cans of corn galore because he’s getting under so many pitches. The real fall-off is relative to last year; his pulled air rate has fallen from 29.5% to 18.5%, while his xSLG has dropped from .464 to .354. As with Altuve and the left field situation, the Astros don’t have great alternatives. Matthews, a 24-year-old rookie, has hit just .201/.255/.332 (64 wRC+), and Meyers sustained a season-ending left kneecap injury at Triple-A Sugar Land last week.
Yet another injury-related note for the Red Sox: Ceddanne Rafaela was sidelined nearly three weeks ago due to a right quad strain. Prior to that, he was putting the finishing touches on a breakout season, having hit .282/.317/.443 (108 wRC+) with 16 homers and 17 steals while playing Gold Glove-caliber defense in center field. Less than a week after he went down, his capable fill-in Eli White suffered a ligament injury in his right foot, requiring season-ending surgery. Since then, Jarren Duran and Nate Eaton have shared the position. Rafaela has yet to return to the roster, though manager Chad Tracy said he’s “getting close.” If he does suffer a setback, continuing to play Duran during what’s been an awful season (.204/.261/.362, 68 wRC+) would obviously be less than ideal.
The Yankees’ Trent Grisham was sidelined by a Grade 2 strain of his right hamstring around the same time that Rafaela went down, and he has yet to return as well. His performance has fallen off drastically after a career year; he’s hit just .211/.308/.395 (98 wRC+) with 18 homers while trading some power for contact, and his defense has also been rough (-5 FRV and -8 DRS in 961.1 innings). While Boone has said he could be “in play at some point” during the postseason, there’s little urgency. Rookie Spencer Jones has shifted over from right field and done an impressive job of holding down the fort, playing adequate defense while hitting .246/.316/.435 (110 wRC+) despite a 36.2% strikeout rate.
Right Field: Heliot Ramos and Aaron Judge, Yankees
Yes, that looks weird in print, but for the moment at least, it’s a reality for the Yankees. The 27-year-old Ramos hit a modest .264/.304/.424 (100 wRC+) with nine homers and 0.6 WAR for the Giants before being traded to the Yankees on August 3. He began his time in pinstripes by going 5-for-47, and at one point went 32 games between homers — from July 20 to August 29 — while slugging .204. He’s heated up since then, but his .168/.294/.356 (85 wRC+) line with the Yankees doesn’t give anyone much confidence he can replace even the banged-up version of Judge the Yankees have received in his 66 games this season (.241/.360/.511, 141 wRC+).
In terms of concerns about sheer replacement-level production, the White Sox stand out here. Early in the season, the team tried Everson Pereira, Jarred Kelenic, and Rikuu Nishida as their regular at the position, but none got the job done. On June 9 they called up Braden Montgomery, a switch-hitting 23-year-old who placed 100th on our Top 100 as a 50-FV prospect in the spring. He collected two hits in his debut that night against the Braves, capped by a walk-off homer, but it’s been mostly downhill since then, as he’s hit .212/.305/.340 (84 wRC+) with six homers and 0.5 WAR in 88 games. While he’s hit .248/.344/.385 (110 wRC+) in 250 plate appearances against righties, he’s flailed away at a .125/.204/.2227 clip in 98 plate appearances against lefties. With resurgent lefty-masher Randal Grichuk on the roster and hitting .331/.372/.650 (182 wRC+) in 172 plate appearances against lefties, there’s no reason that should be happening.
Designated Hitter: Andrew Benintendi, White Sox
No remaining AL contender ranks below 15th in the majors in wRC+ provided by their DHs, and the two lowest teams from among that subset, the Red Sox and Guardians, are respectively third and fourth in second-half wRC+ from that spot while using revolving casts of players. So I’m picking (on) Andrew Benintendi, who has hit a very modest .243/.302/.414 (98 wRC+) while starting at DH in 105 games, with Grichuk (19) the only other Chicago player in double digits. There’s nothing particularly terrible or mysterious about Benintendi’s performance, which beyond a September slump, has lined up with his expected stats quite well; he’s got 21st-percentile bat speed but a 66th-percentile squared-up rate and a 77th-percentile hard-hit rate. He doesn’t hit lefties (.227/.261/.250, 44 wRC+ in 47 PA this year), so manager Will Venable has either used Grichuk or one of his righty regulars there. For as impressive as the White Sox’s turnaround from three straight 100-loss seasons has been, you can see from this roundup that the team’s weaknesses have come to the fore as they’ve tried to sew up a playoff berth.
Brooklyn-based Jay Jaffe is a senior writer for FanGraphs, the author of The Cooperstown Casebook (Thomas Dunne Books, 2017) and the creator of the JAWS (Jaffe WAR Score) metric for Hall of Fame analysis. He founded the Futility Infielder website (2001), was a columnist for Baseball Prospectus (2005-2012) and a contributing writer for Sports Illustrated (2012-2018). He has been a recurring guest on MLB Network and a member of the BBWAA since 2011, and a Hall of Fame voter since 2021. Follow him on BlueSky @jayjaffe.bsky.social.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox clinched their second consecutive playoff berth Sunday and their third since 2021.
It was a season with the highest of highs and the lowest of lows in Boston as they started the season 10-17 before firing longtime manager Alex Cora.
In June, the Red Sox found themselves 14 games under .500 at a record of 32-46. This is when everything changed.
They swept the New York Yankees before losing two out of three games to the Washington Nationals.
The Red Sox went on the road and swept the Los Angeles Angels, Chicago White Sox and New York Mets to sit at 46-48 heading into the all-star break.
After nine straight road wins, the Red Sox headed home to face the 56-38 Tampa Bay Rays. Tampa has had Boston’s number in the past few seasons, but this weekend was different.
In the first game of a doubleheader after the break, the Red Sox took care of business 10-0. Then in the night cap, Tampa Bay Rays took an early 2-0 before outfielder Wilyer Abreu decided the next 24 hours were all about him. He hit two home runs on the way to a 5-3 Red Sox win.
The next game was the defining game of the winning streak. The Rays were matching the Sox in scoring all-game before Abreu stepped to the plate down 6-5 in the seventh. Abreu crushed a two-run homer to right field, sending himself and Fenway Park into a frenzy. His fourth home run in 24 hours put Boston up 7-6, a lead they would hold for 12 consecutive wins.
They swept Tampa the next day before taking the first two games of the series versus the Orioles to tie a franchise record 15 straight wins. That first win did not come without drama. A back-and-forth game was knotted up in the eighth when Caleb Durbin smacked a game winning homerun to left field. The “Durbinator” had a rough start to the season but became one of the centerpieces of this win streak.
The streak would end at 15 but just a week later, Boston would rip off another nine straight wins. Durbin hit a walk-off single in an instant classic 12-11 victory against the White Sox. Ceddanne Rafaela became the king of LA for a few days after smacking four home runs in three games against the back-to-back champs.
So here we are, the Red Sox are 84-72 with a firm grip on the second wild card spot in the American League. Now, the New York Yankees stand in their way.
The Yankees beat the Red Sox 2-1 in the three-game wildcard series last year, and Boston is looking for revenge this season.
The pitching will be the key for both teams. Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez will toe the rubber for Boston against the Yankees’ Gerritt Cole, Max Fried and Massachusetts’ own Cam Schlittler in the series.
In his first full season in the MLB, Tolle hit his stride. The southpaw posted a 3.02 ERA and a 10.4 K/9. He is also peaking at the right time, sporting a 0.75 ERA in two starts during September.
In a complete 180 from Tolle, Gray has been dominant in what may be his swan song in the majors. After being acquired via trade in the offseason, Gray has won 17 games, a career high for the veteran. He pitched 7.1 innings of one hit baseball while striking out nine in a June win over the Yankees.
Suarez signed a 5-year $130 million dollar contract with Boston in the offseason and has been solid as a member of the Sox. However, the 2026 all-star struggled in all three of his starts against the Yankees. The Bronx Bombers were 3-0 against Suarez.
Despite great performances by the Yankees, Suarez is a playoff pitcher. He had a 1.48 ERA in 42.2 postseason innings as a member of the Philadelphia Phillies. In Philadelphia’s 2022 run to the World Series, the Phillies won all five games Suarez pitched in. He only allowed two earned runs in 14.2 innings pitched in 2022.
Along with the starters, the back of the bullpen has been nails for Boston. Erik Miller, Garrett Whitlock and Aroldis Chapman handled the seventh, eighth and ninth innings for interim manager Chad Tracy and the Red Sox. Miller came over at the trade deadline and did not allow an earned run in his first 10 appearances. Whitlock has been a staple in the Red Sox bullpen since 2021 and is possibly having his best year yet. He has a 1.75 ERA in 53 appearances. Chapman continues to age like fine wine. The 38-year-old was named an all-star for the second straight year and is 34/36 in save situations this year.
The rest of the hitters for the Red Sox will need to do some heavy lifting if they want to compete with the Yankees. Boston acquired Adley Rutschman at the deadline, and the catcher will be required to switch hit and catch in the playoffs. Wilson Contreras and Trevor Story will add postseason experience to the lineup while former top prospect Roman Anthony and local legend Mickey Gasper will look to provide during their first playoff at bats.
If the standings hold, the Red Sox and Yankees will battle in the Bronx on Tuesday for the wildcard series, a statement no Red Sox fan would have believed in June.

item.title: [heavy.com] Red Sox SP Payton Tolle Shares Mechanics Concern in Final Regular Season Start
item.dc:creator: Dan Morrison
item.description: The regular season has come to an end for Boston Red Sox starting pitcher Payton Tolle. He made his final scheduled start on Tuesday night, throwing 5.2 innings and giving up 2 earned runs in a no decision against the Cleveland Guardians. There were a couple of reasons being suggested, neither of which would be
item.content:encoded:
The regular season has come to an end for Boston Red Sox starting pitcher Payton Tolle. He made his final scheduled start on Tuesday night, throwing 5.2 innings and giving up 2 earned runs in a no decision against the Cleveland Guardians.
There was some reason for concern in the start, though. Tolle’s velocity was down. In the first inning, he was hitting around 97 mph on the radar gun. By the second, he was around 94 mph.
There were a couple of reasons being suggested, neither of which would be good. He could be dealing with the cold, which going into October isn’t what you want to hear. Or, he could have a mechanical issue, which leads to more questions for the young Red Sox pitcher. For his part, Tolle would blame his mechanics.
“I think there was a little bit of just trying to find my legs for a second,” Tolle said. “I think I got very nitpicky. I got trying to be too fine. It’s like, I don’t — you’re going to see the velo dip whenever I’m being too fine. That’s kind of what happened there, especially with those walks. Just trying too hard on some pitches.”
This comes at a time when Red Sox reliever Erik Miller is battling mechanical issues. Those are issues that have led to concerns about what he can be in the postseason. At the very least, Tolle seemed to figure it out midgame.
“So, it is what it is,” Tolle said. “But I think later I got back to just trying to fly through zone and let it be what it be.”
Boston Red Sox Fans Embraced Payton Tolle in 2026
Boston Red Sox fans got their first taste of Payton Tolle in 2025, but he was still a rookie who started 2026 in the minors. It wouldn’t be until injuries hit the rotation that Tolle made it back to the MLB team, which is a tough spot to be in for anyone. Still, he and the fanbase have seemed to embrace each other.
So, it was no surprise that the Fenway Faithful walked him off the mound on Tuesday with a standing ovation. Unless the Red Sox can win a playoff round, that was his final home game of the season.
Tolle wrapped up the regular season with a 3.03 ERA in 26 games and 148.2 innings. He also had a 1.096 WHIP and 10.4 strikeouts per nine. More importantly, he proved he has secondary pitches beyond his fastball, which is still his bread and butter.
Along the way, Red Sox fans embraced Tolle for how he plays the game. He’s both fiery and passionate, but he doesn’t take himself overly seriously. That has seen him hug runners to tag them out, do push-ups after slipping, and smile before throwing an immaculate inning.
The Red Sox Need Tolle for the Postseason
There is no doubt that the Red Sox are going to need Payton Tolle at his best for the postseason. The question is whether or not he’s getting the ball in Game 1. For his part, manager Chad Tracy didn’t want to give anything away just yet.
“TBD,” Tracy said on when Tolle will pitch next. “But good try, though.”
Tolle only got to pitch 0.1 innings last postseason. The Red Sox need more this year from him, and he’s excited for the opportunity.
“I’m excited… I’ll keep going back to how far we’ve come. Go back to June, and what we were thinking sitting in this same room in June. I’m just really proud of this group; this is incredible. I’ve had so much fun— obviously,” Tolle said.

item.title: [Audacy] The story behind Payton Tolle's viral basketball video
item.dc:creator: Rob Bradford
item.description: As if there needs to be more evidence of Payton Tolle's unique likability, along came a reminder from five years ago. That was courtesy of a video showing Tolle as a basketball player from his days at Bethany High in Bethany, Oklahoma. I present to you: The ultimate Payton Tolle highlight video @BBisntBoring pic.twitter.com/qXSZ3rBz5e — Rob Bradford (@bradfo) September 22, 2026 The images came courtesy of a man who witnessed the Tolle Effect first-hand, former Bethany High boys basketball coach
item.content:encoded:
As if there needs to be more evidence of Payton Tolle's unique likability, along came a reminder from five years ago.
That was courtesy of a video showing Tolle as a basketball player from his days at Bethany High in Bethany, Oklahoma.
I present to you: The ultimate Payton Tolle highlight video @BBisntBoring pic.twitter.com/qXSZ3rBz5e
— Rob Bradford (@bradfo) September 22, 2026
The images came courtesy of a man who witnessed the Tolle Effect first-hand, former Bethany High boys basketball coach Quinn Woolridge. Well before the Red Sox were introduced to the personality of the rookie pitcher, Woolridge experienced the unique existence of the former three-sport athlete.
For instance, that hug he gave Seattle's Dominic Canzone three weeks ago was nothing new. Just ask all those basketball coaches who went up against Woolridge and Bethany High went up against and were greeted with Tolle's signature embrace.The kid just had fun doing everything he was doing. Yeah, that was a chance where he could have some fun.
"All the stuff with the highlights that are coming out now, he always been that fun kid," Woolridge told WEEI.com. "I think you guys are probably getting the feel that he is the genuine article. I mean, he's the real deal."
"It's called a highlight reel for a reason," laughed Tolle when talking about the video, that included the lefty nailing three-pointers and throwing down dunks, along with the consistent hugging of opposing coaches. "A little breakway action never hurt anybody. We had a lot of fun."
And as for the coaches' responses to the embraces, "I would say most like it," Tolle explained. "Some f them tried to get away from it, but I was like, 'No, no, come get this. Let the big bird get his paws on here. Word got around. The Oklahoma high school basketball coaches group is small, so they knew."
The influence his basketball years had on Tolle stretched well beyond just those introductory embraces.
Even though baseball was clearly his meal ticket beyond high school, the 6-foot-5 center made a point to put his all into both football and hoop, two sports Woolridge said Tolle could have also had a future in beyond high school.
"Obviously, baseball was his No. 1 sport," the coach said. "I don't think he really even liked football that much, but he was obivously good at it as a tight end and defensive end. And then he literally played basketball like three months out of the year, but he was pretty good. If he wanted to be a basketball player in college, he could have been. If he wanted to be a tight end, he would have been playing on Saturdays (in college) and maybe even Sundays (in the NFL). Being around him, if he wanted to be good at darts, he would have been really good at darts.
"A lot of young basketball guys, they take themselves too serious. They're into a lot of social media stuff and everything. He was a good basketball player, but he didn't take himself too serious and he had a good time with it. He helped everybody else playing that way, too."
While Tolle wasn't Bethany's leading scorer ("They never ran isolations for me," he joked), he was an important part of a very good team. And as much as his presence did for the Bronchos, the reward was just as great for Tolle to get where he finds himself today.
"Every single time a kid or parent comes up to me and says, 'Hey, what advice do you have for my high school?' I tell them to be an athlete because you're going to learn movements and explosiveness. I might not show it out there anymore, but I would say that a lot. Not to too my own horn, but I feel l ike I move fine for a large guy thanks to the base athleticism that was happening in other sports.
"(By playing one sport) you're going to find yourself burned out. You're going to find yourself overusing your muscles over and over again. With basketball, I knew once Christmas and New Year's happened I would go back to throwing after basketball practice, just stacking days. It helped me be an athlete and not get too burnt going to baseball all the time. There's also a lot of mental stuff that goes into, too."
Now, we have the memories, the impact of those days on the basketball court, and a pretty enlightening video montage.
"The biggest thing is he was such a competitor," remembered Woolridge. "He was such a positive influence with all the guys on our team. That was one of my prevailing memories about him.
"You see a lot of guys that have a good PR team that puts good stuff out there about them, and then you meet them in an elevator and they're kind of a turd. What you see with Payton that is out there now is what you get from him every single day, and what he was at Bethany High."

item.dc:creator: Scott Martin
item.description: BOSTON — Nathaniel Lowe had a tiebreaking sacrifice fly off reliever Erik Miller in the ninth inning, and the Cleveland Guardians maintained their slim in the AL Central with a 3-2 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Tuesday night. Angel Martínez had three hits for the Guardians, who entered the day with a one-game lead over the White Sox atop the division. Chicago owns the tiebreaker by winning the season series. Cleveland stranded 15 baserunners. The loss was Boston’s eighth in 12 games, spoili
item.content:encoded:
BOSTON — Nathaniel Lowe had a tiebreaking sacrifice fly off reliever Erik Miller in the ninth inning, and the Cleveland Guardians maintained their slim in the AL Central with a 3-2 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Tuesday night.
Angel Martínez had three hits for the Guardians, who entered the day with a one-game lead over the White Sox atop the division. Chicago owns the tiebreaker by winning the season series. Cleveland stranded 15 baserunners.
The loss was Boston’s eighth in 12 games, spoiling Chad Tracy’s first game as manager after the club named him its 49th in team history.
Adley Rutschman added three hits for Boston, which clinched one of the AL’s wild-card spots on Sunday.
Boston pinch hitter Mickey Gasper hit Hunter Gaddis’ first pitch, tying it at 2-2 leading off the eighth.
Gaddis (5-3) got the win and Cade Smith recorded the final three outs for his 40th save.
Miller (4-2) hit a batter and gave up two hits in an inning.
A strong candidate for the AL Rookie of the Year, Cleveland left-hander Parker Messick gave up a run over five innings. He lowered his ERA to 2.55 and is on pace to become the fourth rookie starting pitcher in MLB history with an ERA under 2.60 and averaging 9.0 or more strikeouts per nine innings.
In his tune-up for a likely playoff start next week, Boston lefty Payton Tolle struggled with his control over 5 2/3 innings, giving up two runs on eight hits.
Up next
Guardians LHP Foster Griffin (15-5, 3.67 ERA) is set to face Red Sox RHP Sonny Gray (17-5, 2.82) on Wednesday in the middle game of the three-game series.

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

23 Sep 2026, 07:35 GMT+10

(Photo credit: David Butler II)
Nathaniel Lowe hit a sacrifice fly to right field that drove in Chase DeLauter in the ninth inning and the visiting Cleveland Guardians held on to beat the Boston Red Sox 3-2 Tuesday in the first game of a three-game series.
Boston's Erik Miller (4-2) walked one and allowed two hits in the ninth.
Hunter Gaddis (5-3) got the win despite allowing a game-tying home run to Mickey Gasper in the eighth. Cade Smith pitched a scoreless ninth to record his 40th save. The victory extended Cleveland's winning streak to six games as it maintained its one-game lead over the Chicago White Sox in the AL Central.
Parker Messick held Boston to one run on five hits in five innings. He struck out five and walked one. Messick has allowed three runs or fewer in each of his last 14 starts.
Payton Tolle started for the Red Sox (84-73) and gave up two runs on eight hits in 5 2/3 innings. He walked two and struck out five.
Adley Rutschman had three hits for the Red Sox, who had eight hits in the game.
Cleveland's Angel Martinez went 3-for-4 and scored a run. The Guardians (82-75) received two hits from DeLauter, who reached in the ninth when Miller hit him with a pitch.
The Guardians went 1-for-12 with runners in scoring position and stranded 15.
The Guardians took a 2-0 lead in the second. Martinez doubled and made it 1-0 when he scored on David Fry's single. Fry doubled the lead by scoring when Brayan Rocchio grounded into a 4-6-3 double play.
Boston trimmed its deficit to 2-1 in the second. Rutschman led off with a double, moved to third on Caleb Durbin's groundout to second and scored on Andrew Monasterio's groundout to shortstop.
Gasper's home run, his 10th of the year, tied the game leading off the eighth.
Boston stranded the tying run on second in the ninth as Smith retired Nick Sogard on a grounder to second.
--Field Level Media
