item.title: [The Boston Globe] Postseason secured, but Red Sox trending in wrong direction and Guardians take advantage to open series - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Tim Healey
item.description: In this purgatorial period for the Red Sox, after they clinched a playoff berth over the weekend and before they open the postseason next week, what matters? The result Tuesday, a 3-2 loss to the Guardians at Fenway Park, was not of major significance. Of greater note was the how — and what those trends may portend heading into the most important time of year: another ugly outing for reliever Erik Miller, and another night of minimal hitting for the lineup. The Red Sox (84-73) have dropped three
item.content:encoded:
In this purgatorial period for the Red Sox, after they clinched a playoff berth over the weekend and before they open the postseason next week, what matters?
The result Tuesday, a 3-2 loss to the Guardians at Fenway Park, was not of major significance.
Of greater note was the how — and what those trends may portend heading into the most important time of year: another ugly outing for reliever Erik Miller, and another night of minimal hitting for the lineup.
The Red Sox (84-73) have dropped three games in a row and eight of their past 12.
“We’ve still got five games to play, and you [have to] keep guys out there and engaged and ready to roll,” manager Chad Tracy said. “I told the guys before, we earned the right to be in position to be able to line things up. That being said, we still want to go out and win the games. We had a chance to tonight.”
Miller inherited a tied game in the ninth inning and struggled again, allowing a game-deciding run and throwing 22 pitches (10 strikes). He hit his first batter, Chase DeLauter, with a pitch. DeLauter eventually scored on Nathaniel Lowe’s sacrifice fly. Altogether, Miller yielded two hits and a walk.
In September, the Sox’ theoretical top lefthanded setup man has one clean inning in seven attempts, a 8.53 ERA, and a 2.37 WHIP.
Miller said his patience with himself — and a mechanical issue he is trying to fix — is “definitely running thin at this point.”
“I’d be lying if I say otherwise,” he said. “I would like to have been through this by now, be over it. But … there’s no way I can feel better and work through it without throwing [in] a game. So that’s just how it’s going to have to be: keep throwing, get through it.”
Tracy, noting that Miller will pitch in a couple more games before the regular season ends Sunday, added: “I thought today was even another step in the right direction.”
Offensively, the Red Sox had few highlights. Mickey Gasper launched a pinch-hit tying home run off setup man Hunter Gaddis to lead off the eighth, but the Sox totaled nine runners stranded on base and went 0 for 9 with men in scoring position.
In the positives column: Adley Rutschman finished 3 for 4, with two doubles (and a line out to deep center) coming against lefthanders.
Entering the game, Rutschman was 2 for 26 with no extra-base hits against lefties as a member of the Red Sox.
“Being a switch hitter has a lot that goes into it, and you go through phases where you’re hitting good [from] one side and not the other and it flip flops sometimes and then goes back,” Rutschman said. “I want to be in a good spot, especially with the playoffs coming up.”
In a matchup between perhaps the top two rookie pitchers this year, Payton Tolle (5⅔ innings, two runs) was almost equal to fellow lefthander Parker Messick (five innings, one run) of the Guardians.
Tolle slogged through a 22-pitch second frame, during which he allowed three hits and two walks but managed to hold the AL Central-leading Guardians (82-75) to the two runs.
When Tracy pulled him in the sixth, Tolle walked off the Fenway mound — for potentially the last time this year — to a standing ovation from the fans behind the home dugout. He waved back to them.
“I think he’s won them over pretty significantly,” Tracy said.
Tolle finished his rookie season with a 3.03 ERA and 171 strikeouts in 148⅔ innings (26 starts).
Up next: a start in the AL Wild Card Series.
“It’s the postseason. This is what we play for,” Tolle said. “But it is what it is. We go on, and we have a job to do.”
Tim Healey can be reached at timothy.healey@globe.com. Follow him @timbhealey.

item.title: [MLB.com] Tolle puts bow on standout rookie season with October spotlight looming
item.dc:creator: Ian Browne
item.description: BOSTON -- When Payton Tolle walked off the mound with two outs in the top of the sixth inning on Tuesday night, it was the perfect opportunity for the Fenway faithful to recognize the power lefty for an outstanding rookie season. Next time Tolle pitches, the noise is likely to be even louder, and not nearly as favorable. The Red Sox will have no hesitation sending out the confident, charismatic 23-year-old into enemy territory. While this was far from the best (5 2/3 innings, 8 hits, 2 ER, 2 BBs
item.content:encoded:
BOSTON -- When Payton Tolle walked off the mound with two outs in the top of the sixth inning on Tuesday night, it was the perfect opportunity for the Fenway faithful to recognize the power lefty for an outstanding rookie season.
Next time Tolle pitches, the noise is likely to be even louder, and not nearly as favorable.
The Red Sox will have no hesitation sending out the confident, charismatic 23-year-old into enemy territory.
While this was far from the best (5 2/3 innings, 8 hits, 2 ER, 2 BBs, 5 K’s) of Tolle’s 26 regular-season starts, it was more than enough to keep the Red Sox in the game.
Assuming Tolle doesn’t pitch again in the regular season, his final stat line includes this: A 3.03 ERA, 171 strikeouts, 40 walks, 1.10 WHIP and a .222 opponents batting average.
Playing short-handed without Willson Contreras (bruised knuckle, right hand), Ceddanne Rafaela (right quadriceps strain, 10-day IL) and Trevor Story (rest), the Red Sox continued their recent trend of not scoring much.
There were two bright spots.
Mickey Gasper came up as a pinch-hitter and hammered a game-tying solo shot to right in the bottom of the eighth.
Adley Rutschman, who had been slumping of late, belted two doubles as part of a three-hit night.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Erik Miller gives up lead in ninth as Red Sox lose third straight
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: For all intents and purposes, none of these last games down the stretch mean anything to the Red Sox. They have already punched their ticket to the playoffs and nothing that happens from here on out will change that. But while readying themselves for the games that matter, the Red Sox would still prefer to go into the postseason with some momentum, and Tuesday’s performance was at times pretty hard to watch. Playing without three projected postseason starters, the Red Sox suffered a listless 3-2
item.content:encoded:
For all intents and purposes, none of these last games down the stretch mean anything to the Red Sox. They have already punched their ticket to the playoffs and nothing that happens from here on out will change that.
But while readying themselves for the games that matter, the Red Sox would still prefer to go into the postseason with some momentum, and Tuesday’s performance was at times pretty hard to watch.
Playing without three projected postseason starters, the Red Sox suffered a listless 3-2 loss in their series opener against the Cleveland Guardians. Despite a game-tying pinch hit home run by Mickey Gasper in the bottom of the eighth, the Red Sox gave the lead right back in the ninth, capping off a night riddled with poor decisions and uncharacteristic mistakes.
Reliever Erik Miller saw his struggles continue by allowing two hits, a walk, a hit batsman and the go-ahead sacrifice fly by Angel Martinez in the top of the ninth, and outside of Gasper and Adley Rutschman going 3 for 4 with two doubles and a run scored, there wasn’t much to write home about as the Red Sox suffered their third straight defeat.
Making his final start before the playoffs, Payton Tolle wasn’t as sharp as he would’ve hoped, but once again he gave the Red Sox a chance to win.
After posting a scoreless first, Tolle allowed two runs and five baserunners over the course of a challenging second inning. He started by giving up a leadoff double, had a soft grounder from David Fry deflect off his leg and into the outfield for an RBI single, and allowed another single and a walk to load the bases with nobody out.
Tolle was able to minimize the damage from there, allowing a second run to score on a double play ball by Brayan Rocchio before escaping the inning. He continued facing traffic for the rest of his outing but grinded his way into the sixth and departed to a standing ovation from the Fenway Park faithful.
Tolle finished with two runs allowed on eight hits, two walks and a hit batsman over 5 2/3 innings with five strikeouts. He fell one out short of recording another quality start, leaving him with 13 in 26 outings, and he ends his rookie year with a 3.03 ERA and 171 strikeouts in 148 2/3 innings.
The Red Sox got a run back in the bottom of the second after Adley Rutschman led off with a double and came around to score on an RBI groundout by Andruw Monasterio, but otherwise the bats struggled against Guardians rookie Parker Messick. The left-hander, who came into the game with a 2.57 ERA and projects as a possible AL Cy Young Award finalist, limited the Red Sox to one run on five hits over five innings.
One thing Boston was able to do was drive up the rookie’s pitch count, particularly in the fourth when Monasterio was able to work a 12-pitch walk. That helped force the lefty from the game after five, giving the Red Sox a chance to try their luck against Cleveland’s bullpen.
The Red Sox let a golden opportunity go to waste in the bottom of the sixth, leaving men at second and third, but Alec Gamboa kept it a one-run game in the top of the seventh despite the Guardians taking advantage of some sloppy baseball to get runners at second and third themselves with one out.
Cleveland’s Fry, who had already grounded into a fielder’s choice where the runner was thrown out at the plate earlier in the third inning, did so a second time for the second out of the seventh, and Gamboa struck out former No. 1 overall pick Travis Bazzana to end the inning.
Then, in the bottom of the eighth, Gasper struck for his 10th home run of the season, hitting the first pitch he saw from Guardians reliever Hunter Gaddis 390 feet to the right field stands.
The good vibes didn’t last long.
Miller, who had proven an impactful bullpen addition since his arrival at the trade deadline, saw his recent control issues continue with his latest ugly outing. The left-hander hit the first batter he faced, gave up the lead on a sacrifice fly by Martinez and eventually loaded the bases before getting a fly out to keep things from spiraling further.
Miller has now allowed six runs and six walks over his past 3 1/3 innings, a trend the Red Sox can’t afford to continue if he’s to remain a high-leverage option in the playoffs.

Boston clinched their spot in the postseason after the Atlanta Braves completed a three-game sweep of the Houston Astros on Sunday afternoon. item.content:encoded:
After an off day on Monday, the Boston Red Sox will return to Fenway Park to begin the next-to-last series of the regular season before the playoffs next week. Boston clinched their spot in the postseason after the Atlanta Braves completed a three-game sweep of the Houston Astros on Sunday afternoon.
The Red Sox are all but locked into the second American League wild-card spot. They are on a collision course with the New York Yankees next week in the Bronx for a best-of-three series. Before then, however, Boston has three games with the Cleveland Guardians. They will then host the Chicago Cubs this weekend, weather permitting.
As for the Guardians series, Wilyer Abreu is back in the lineup for manager Chad Tracy and batting in a familiar spot.
Boston Red Sox Announce Wilyer Abreu Spot in Lineup Against Guardians on Tuesday Night
Tracy will send left-hander Payton Tolle to the mound to open the series and as far as his lineup goes, Abreu us back and batting cleanup. Here is Boston's lineup for the series opener against Cleveland's Parker Messick,
Nick Sogard 1B
Jahmai Jones DH
Wilyer Abreu RF
Caleb Durbin 3B
Isiah Kiner-Falefa SS
Nate Eaton CF
Abreu will be batting fourth, with first baseman Willson Contreras still out of the lineup after getting hit by a pitch last Thursday night against the Texas Rangers. He missed the series against the Tampa Bay Rays. As for Abreu, he did not play in Sunday's series finale, a 5-1 loss.
Boston Red Sox Playing Out the String Ahead of Playoffs
Tuesday, it was announced that Tracy was having the interim tag removed, and Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow is having his option in 2029 and 2030 picked up by the club. It's not surprising that it was announced before the playoffs.
Boston is scheduled to send their three projected starters on the mound next week against the Yankees: Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suárez against the Guardians. However, Cleveland is in a heated race with the Chicago White Sox for the American League Central Division title. They enter the series with a one-game lead over the White Sox, who are playing the Kansas City Royals this week.
Boston has slumped in September. However, they can use the six games before next week as a tune-up. As for this weekend, the weather is projected to be a mess. Tim Healy of the Boston Globe reported that MLB has no plans to move the series out of Boston. There are going to be very few windows to play baseball this weekend.
The Cubs are in a battle for home-field advantage in the National League wild-card round. Those games will have big meaning for them and the NL. They enter play this week tied with the San Diego Padres for home-field advantage next week. The Philadelphia Phillies are a game behind. There is a lot riding on this weekend.

item.title: [bosoxinjection.com] Red Sox’s rotation against Guardians could preview Wild Card Game 1 starter fans desperately want
item.dc:creator: Katie Manganelli
item.description: The postseason begins on September 29, giving teams one day of rest between the end of the regular season and the start of the race. Playoff teams must plan their rotations early have the right pitchers rested and ready for the opening series and the Boston Red Sox have seemingly made their call. The Red Sox's rotation for their upcoming matchup with the Cleveland Guardians, their second-to-last series of the year, is Payton Tolle in game one, Sonny Gray in game two and Ranger Suarez in game thr
item.content:encoded:
The postseason begins on September 29, giving teams one day of rest between the end of the regular season and the start of the race. Playoff teams must plan their rotations early have the right pitchers rested and ready for the opening series and the Boston Red Sox have seemingly made their call.
The Red Sox's rotation for their upcoming matchup with the Cleveland Guardians, their second-to-last series of the year, is Payton Tolle in game one, Sonny Gray in game two and Ranger Suarez in game three. That leaves Patrick Sandoval, Jake Bennett and Brayan Bello (or a bullpen game) for the final series against the Chicago Cubs, not necessarily in that order.
Tolle has earned the series-opening start against the New York Yankees. He's posted a 2.36 ERA and 0.88 WHIP with 56 strikeouts over his last seven starts. He's stayed hot despite having 143 innings on his arm this year, and he's gotten even better as the year has gone on.
Tolle has had previous success against the Yankees, including two stellar outings this year. He faced the Yankees in his first big league appearance this year and allowed just one run on three hits with 11 strikeouts and a walk over six innings. Tolle next faced New York on June 26 (one of the games in the four-game sweep that started Boston's historic summer winning streak) and he pitched seven, one-hit innings with seven strikeouts.
Red Sox-Guardians series likely previews Boston's Wild Card rotation with Payton Tolle starting Game 1
Starting Tolle first could set up a battle between two young lefties and Cy Young Award contenders (though it isn't much of a contest) if the Yankees plan to open the series with their ace Cam Schlittler. This might not be the case, though, as New York seems to be setting Gerrit Cole up for the Game 1 start. The Red Sox don't fare as well against right-handed pitching as they do against lefties, with a .712 team OPS against them, and taking Boston off its game will be a high priority for its rival.
Whether the Red Sox win or lose Game 1, Game 2 means everything. With a series loss or a sweep on the line, Boston's ace Gray should take the mound. The 36-year-old Gray has surprised fans everywhere by posting one of the best seasons of his career with the Red Sox and his consistency is unmatched.
Gray has clocked a 2.82 ERA, 1.16 WHIP, 146 strikeouts and 45 walks over 163 innings. Like the Red Sox, the Yankees also don't perform especially well against righty pitching, with a .713 OPS as a club. With a sweep on the line or to stay alive, the veteran Gray is the guy to trust.
In a win-or-go-home Game 3, Suarez deserves Boston's trust. He's gotten back on his feet over the last few weeks following a shaky spell (5.70 ERA in August) after a groin injury. Postseason starts are Suarez's bread and butter — he boasts a 1.48 ERA and 1.06 WHIP over 42.2 frames across seven playoff series — and he's the best choice to keep the Red Sox alive when they're on the brink of elimination.
Boston's rotation has been the biggest strength of the team all season. With these three pitchers, in any order, the Red Sox have good chances to get past the Yankees to advance to the Division Series. But setting the energy with Tolle and having the two veterans follow, as Boston has set things up, makes a lot of sense.

Regardless of how the Sox choose to stack the deck, this will be Tolle’s final tune up before
item.content:encoded:
Chad Tracy told us not to look very much into the order of the rotation this week, but it’s hard not to note that Payton Tolle is starting tonight exactly one week before the Wild Card series begins, and Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez are set to go tomorrow and Thursday. That feels like a Game 1, Game 2, and Game 3 setup for New York, but again, we’ll still have to wait a few more days for official word.
Regardless of how the Sox choose to stack the deck, this will be Tolle’s final tune up before the showdown against the Yankees, so how he looks here will be even more important than the result of this game for the Red Sox.
On the contrary, this game means everything to Cleveland. Despite entering the night three games behind the Red Sox, they’re currently leading the AL Central by a game over the Chicago White Sox, and if the season ended today, they’d actually get a bye and wouldn’t even have to play in the Wild Card round.
To help them maintain control of that bye, they have their ace Parker Messick on the mound, who enters the evening with a 2.57 ERA and 186 strike outs on the season.
Switching gears to the Red Sox lineup, the biggest note is that Roman Anthony is again in left field and Jarren Duran starts the night on the bench. This is becoming the theme against left handed starts, which is obviously noteworthy for next week because Carlos Rodon and Max Fried are both left handed.

item.content:encoded:
With just a few games remaining in the regular season, the chances of a Red Sox vs. Yankees matchup in the AL Wild Card round appear high.
If the Rays can officially clinch the AL East, and the Red Sox can pull away from the White Sox for the AL's No. 5 seed, Boston will be traveling to face New York in a best-of-three matchup.
So when Aaron Boone announced the latest on Aaron Judge's injury status on Tuesday, it carried massive implications for the Red Sox as they begin looking toward the postseason.
Here's the latest on Judge and what it could mean for the Red Sox.
How Yankees' Aaron Judge Injury Update Affects Red Sox
On Tuesday, Boone told reporters that Judge, who was recently played on the 10-day IL with a calf strain just days after his return from a significant injury, is dealing with a "moderate grade" strain.
However, more significantly, Boone said the Yankees aren't preparing for Judge to be ready for the start of the postseason after he had a PPP injection on Monday.
"We’re planning on him not being a part of that,” Boone said, per Bryan Hoch.
While Judge's status for a likely wild-card matchup won't become official until early next week, when the Yankees would have to finalize their roster for a series, it's looking unlikely that he will be healthy in time.
For the Red Sox, no Judge would change the dynamic of attacking the Yankees' lineup. While Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger remain power threats themselves, the presence of the three-time AL MVP boosts New York's offense to an elite status. Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle — likely to pitch for Boston in a best-of-three series — wouldn't have to worry about the threat of Judge's bat breaking a game open in one swing.
Red Sox vs. Yankees is not yet official, and neither is Judge's status for the postseason. But as of Tuesday, all indications are that New York will have to host Boston without its superstar outfielder.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox Get Ceddanne Rafaela Update Ahead of Guardians Series
item.dc:creator: Keith Watkins
item.description: The Boston Red Sox have scored 2.82 runs per game across their last 11 outings. The lineup is collectively batting .210 and posting a .621 OPS in that span. Wilyer Abreu, Adley Rutschman, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, and Nick Sogard have all gone cold at the wrong time. The Latest on Rafaela Ceddanne Rafaela is expected to return to th
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have scored 2.82 runs per game across their last 11 outings. The lineup is collectively batting .210 and posting a .621 OPS in that span. Wilyer Abreu, Adley Rutschman, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, and Nick Sogard have all gone cold at the wrong time.
With the Wild Card Series beginning September 29, the Red Sox need their bats to wake up before October arrives.
The cavalry is coming. And the timing could not be better.
The Latest on Rafaela
Ceddanne Rafaela is expected to return to the lineup on Tuesday when the Red Sox open a three-game series against the Guardians at Fenway Park.
The All-Star center fielder has been sidelined for 16 games since straining his right quadriceps.
Chad Tracy indicated over the weekend that Rafaela should come off the injured list for the homestand. The rotation is set up with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez, a sequence that mirrors how the staff could be deployed in the Wild Card Series.
Getting Rafaela back before those games begin gives him a chance to find his timing and reintegrate into the lineup before the stakes get higher.
What Rafaela Brings Back
Rafaela's absence has been felt. On the season, he has produced 16 home runs, 70 RBIs, and a .282/.760 line. His combination of contact, power, and speed makes him one of the most complete players on the roster.
The defensive impact is equally significant. Rafaela's range in center field changes the way the pitching staff operates. Fly balls that fall for hits with other outfielders become outs when he is patrolling the middle of the outfield. His presence there tightens the entire defense.
The Red Sox have been using Jarren Duran and Nate Eaton to fill the void in center. Both have been serviceable, but neither provides the combination of offense and defense that Rafaela delivers on a daily basis.
The Red Sox Offense Needs a Spark
The numbers paint a clear picture of how badly the Red Sox have struggled at the plate.
Mickey Gasper is 4-for-25 over the recent stretch. Kiner-Falefa has managed just one hit in his last 20 at-bats. Sogard is 8-for-40. The lineup has lacked the consistent production that fueled the summer surge.
There have been bright spots. Roman Anthony broke out of a prolonged slump with a 5-for-13 weekend against the Rays that included two doubles and a homer. Trevor Story has been one of the hottest hitters on the roster since returning from the injured list, carrying a .338 average with an .869 OPS across 19 games.
Willson Contreras is also working his way back from a bruised right hand and could return this week. If both Contreras and Rafaela rejoin the lineup for the Guardians series, it would be the healthiest the Red Sox' batting order has looked in weeks.
Final Word for the Red Sox
The Red Sox have six games left before the playoffs begin.
Rafaela's return gives the lineup a jolt it needs. What he provides on both sides of the ball is invaluable for Boston.
Fenway awaits.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Ranger Suarez’s antics cement his perfect playoff mentality after Red Sox clinch
item.dc:creator: Brian Burrows
item.description: Ranger Suarez is back to having fun after clinching the playoffs. Despite losing on Sunday, the Boston Red Sox clinched their spot in the postseason due to other teams' losses. The Sox took a team picture on the field at Tropicana Field before heading into the clubhouse for the usual champagne showers and beer. In the team photo, Suarez clearly sticks out. Standing right in the middle, the lefty starter had bright red shorts pulled up well above his waist, and his celebratory shirt tucked in. He
item.content:encoded:
Ranger Suarez is back to having fun after clinching the playoffs. Despite losing on Sunday, the Boston Red Sox clinched their spot in the postseason due to other teams' losses. The Sox took a team picture on the field at Tropicana Field before heading into the clubhouse for the usual champagne showers and beer.
In the team photo, Suarez clearly sticks out. Standing right in the middle, the lefty starter had bright red shorts pulled up well above his waist, and his celebratory shirt tucked in. He was also the only player in the picture with his goggles already covering his eyes. Suarez was known as a fun celebration guy with the Philadelphia Phillies, and it was something the fans there loved about him; Red Sox Nation was just waiting to see in Boston.
While Suarez is all fun and games with good spirits during a celebration, he does a complete 180 once the playoffs start. He's been one of the best playoff pitchers ever. His 1.48 ERA is the sixth-lowest of all time among pitchers with at least 40 innings pitched in the playoffs.
The 31-year-old has pitched in each of the last four postseasons. In 2023, he allowed just two earned runs in 14 2/3 innings. In 2024, he allowed four earned runs in 18 2/3 innings. In 2024, he allowed no runs in 4 1/3 innings. In 2025, he allowed one earned run in five innings. In the regular season, the lefty has a career 8.4 K/9; in the playoffs, it's 9.3
Ranger Suarez's playoff pedigree should excite fans after last season's playoff rotation
His playoff excellence was part of the reason the Red Sox signed him. While Suarez has been a very solid regular-season pitcher, it was his success in the playoffs that really made him stand out in last season's free-agent pool. After Garrett Crochet, the Red Sox ended up relying on Brayan Bello and Connelly Early. The Sox knew they needed another playoff-tested arm for the postseason and made the splash signing of the lefty to do so.
The Red Sox now head into the 2026 playoffs with a projected Wild Card round rotation that will consist of Suarez, Sonny Gray, and Payton Tolle. While the exact order is yet to be determined, those three arms will instill much more confidence than the three who started the games last year.
Suarez likes to have his fun. He did so in Philly and is doing so again here in Boston. That doesn't mean that opponents should take him lightly. Come playoff time, Suarez turns it on and shuts down the other teams.

item.title: [nesn.com] Chad Tracy Delivers Powerful Message After Red Sox Clinch Playoff Spot | NESN
item.dc:creator: Rodney Knuppel
item.description: The Boston Red Sox did not clinch their postseason berth with a dramatic walk-off hit or a dominant performance from their pitching staff. They clinched after losing 5-1 to the Tampa Bay Rays and receiving help from Mike Yastrzemski and the Atlanta Braves. Interim manager Chad Tracy did not care how the ticket was punched. “When you work as hard as we have worked, I don’t think you care much how it gets done,” Tracy told reporters. “You just want to see your ticket get punched.” That message per
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox did not clinch their postseason berth with a dramatic walk-off hit or a dominant performance from their pitching staff. They clinched after losing 5-1 to the Tampa Bay Rays and receiving help from Mike Yastrzemski and the Atlanta Braves.
Interim manager Chad Tracy did not care how the ticket was punched.
“When you work as hard as we have worked, I don’t think you care much how it gets done,” Tracy told reporters. “You just want to see your ticket get punched.”
That message perfectly captured Boston’s remarkable season. The Red Sox were 32-46 and appeared destined to spend the summer discussing trades, organizational changes and another disappointing finish. Instead, they became the first team in MLB history to finish above .500 and reach the playoffs after losing at least 46 of its first 78 games.
“They didn’t take no for an answer,” Tracy said.
Where It Started
Tracy inherited a 10-17 team when the Red Sox moved on from Alex Cora in April. There was no immediate transformation, and Boston’s season continued to drift for several weeks.
Eventually, everything changed. Boston swept four games from the New York Yankees at Fenway Park in late June and began one of the most impressive turnarounds in franchise history. Young players developed into meaningful contributors, the clubhouse remained together and the Red Sox kept finding ways to survive injuries.
The result is a second consecutive postseason appearance and another likely Wild Card Series against the Yankees. That matchup did not work out for Boston last October. The Red Sox won the opener behind Garrett Crochet but dropped the next two games in New York.
This year’s roster has traveled a much different road.
The Red Sox have played meaningful baseball for months because almost every loss threatened to undo the progress they had made. Players such as Roman Anthony, Payton Tolle and Connelly Early have grown up in that environment, while veterans including Trevor Story and Willson Contreras helped keep the clubhouse steady.
Getting Things Set Up
Now Boston has an opportunity to set its rotation, protect tired relievers and enter the postseason with more than a week to prepare. The final regular-season games still matter, especially with the Cleveland Guardians visiting Fenway Park. Boston can use the series to evaluate potential postseason matchups and determine which pitchers are best equipped for important October innings.
The celebration also strengthens Tracy’s case to remain manager beyond this season. Boston did not merely improve after he took control. The Red Sox completed a turnaround that had never been accomplished in major league history.
Tracy did not want credit Sunday. His message remained focused on the players who refused to allow a terrible start to define them. That approach may be one of the biggest reasons the Red Sox are still playing.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Decisions, decisions: Five questions for Red Sox to answer before playoffs
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: The Red Sox are officially headed back to the postseason, and by clinching a spot with more than a week to spare, the club now has the luxury of making all of its playoff preparations without stressing about the final six-game homestand. But there’s still unfinished business to attend to, so here are a few loose threads the Red Sox need to address before Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series next Tuesday. Who starts Game 1? When the Red Sox return to Fenway Park for this week’s penultim
item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox are officially headed back to the postseason, and by clinching a spot with more than a week to spare, the club now has the luxury of making all of its playoff preparations without stressing about the final six-game homestand.
But there’s still unfinished business to attend to, so here are a few loose threads the Red Sox need to address before Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series next Tuesday.
Who starts Game 1?
When the Red Sox return to Fenway Park for this week’s penultimate series against the Cleveland Guardians, they will send Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez to the mound, in that order.
Could that be a preview of the AL Wild Card Series rotation? Maybe, but not necessarily.
It’s a testament to the season Tolle has enjoyed that he’s a realistic choice to start Game 1. The rookie left-hander has been fantastic all season, posting a 3.02 ERA over 143 innings through 25 starts, and he’s been especially impressive as the season has gone along.
Gray and Suarez are obviously the more experienced options, but if Tolle is capable of delivering a shutdown playoff performance like Garrett Crochet last fall, there’s merit in sending him out as soon as possible rather than waiting for a do-or-die Game 3 scenario.
If not Tolle, Gray is the obvious choice to start Game 1. Gray has been the ace of the staff ever since Crochet went down in April, and starting the veteran right off the bat would also allow the Red Sox to throw Tolle or Suarez on extra rest no matter which order they chose.
Bello or Bennett as long man?
If there’s a player whose individual season best parallels the 2026 Red Sox, it might be Brayan Bello.
Coming into the year as one of Boston’s longest-tenured starters, Bello completely imploded and lost not just his spot in the Red Sox rotation but his place on the big league roster entirely. But since returning from Triple-A just before the All-Star break, Bello has been fantastic, and last time out he delivered one of the best starts of his career, striking out 11 over eight dominant innings.
Between that and another strong showing against the Angels earlier this month, it appears Bello has finally gotten past whatever issues he was having in the first inning early on. Given that Jake Bennett has been a bit shaky recently, the Red Sox may need to consider the possibility that Bello might actually be the club’s best option as the No. 4 starter should the Red Sox advance to the ALDS.
But there are other factors to consider, too.
With the club only needing three starters for the best-of-three Wild Card series, it would make sense for the Red Sox to leave their No. 4 starter off the wild card roster so they can be lined up and fresh for Game 1 of the ALDS. Since Bennett has never pitched out of the bullpen in his MLB career, and Bello has proven quite adept in that role, it would make sense to stick with Bennett as the No. 4 starter and roster Bello as the long man.
But on the flip side, carrying three starters means the Red Sox won’t need a No. 5 starter either, which means they can add a ninth short-inning reliever on top of the long-man. With all hands on deck and presumably Tolle, Gray and Suarez capable of going deep into the game, the Red Sox could prioritize keeping the preferred Game 1 ALDS starter in reserve, in which case having Bennett as the emergency arm wouldn’t be the end of the world.
Will any rehabbing arms make roster?
With extra spots in the bullpen up for grabs, the Red Sox have to decide if any of their rehabbing arms have progressed to a point where they’re a better option than some of the club’s lower-leverage relievers.
Tanner Houck seems to be the most likely candidate for a bullpen spot at this point. He’s made four appearances out of the bullpen in the minors since the start of September, alternating between 20-pitch short outings and 40-pitch bulk appearances. With the minor league season over and a playoff spot clinched, it wouldn’t be a surprise to see Houck activated this week to pitch in the final homestand, which would both allow the clubs higher leverage arms to stay fresh and potentially serve as a playoff audition for Houck.
How about Crochet? He would almost certainly be limited to one inning at a time, but he also hasn’t faced live hitters yet. If Crochet throws live batting practice this week and comes out looking good, it’s possible the Red Sox could make a bet on his immense upside, though, if the club is serious about not rushing him back it might make sense to hold off until at least the ALDS.
Two longer-shot candidates that can’t be completely ruled out are Johan Oviedo and Kutter Crawford. Oviedo made his first in-game appearance since March last week, throwing 2 1/3 innings for the WooSox in a rehab outing, and Crawford was scheduled to pitch Sunday’s season finale for Worcester before that game was rained out. It would be a surprise if either factors into the playoff picture, but they could conceivably make cameos in Boston this week to help cover some innings down the stretch.
Who will be last man on bench?
The Red Sox are going to have to make some tough decisions when it comes to constructing their bench. Assuming the club carries a back-up catcher — probably Connor Wong — they’ll only have three additional spots and more than a half dozen candidates to fill them.
For starters, which of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Romy Gonzalez will serve as the primary back-up right-handed infielder. Would the Red Sox carry two of the three? Or just one to make room for Jahmai Jones as the lefty-killing pinch hitter and emergency outfielder?
How about Mickey Gasper? He’s been one of the club’s best hitters since mid-August and would provide a potent left-handed weapon to use in a late-inning spot against a big righty reliever.
And lastly, do the Red Sox reserve a spot for a dedicated pinch runner like Dave Roberts back in 2004? If so, then maybe Braiden Ward, who just stole 61 bases for the WooSox, might have a chance to make his MLB debut in the playoffs.
Will Mother Nature throw a curveball?
Before the Red Sox even get to the playoffs, they may have to navigate a messy weather situation.
As of this writing, the forecasts indicate a nor’easter could bring heavy rain, gusty winds and coastal flooding to the Boston area throughout the weekend. That is not conducive to playing outdoor baseball, and while the Red Sox probably won’t have anything to play for, the series could have big ramifications for the Chicago Cubs and the National League Wild Card race.
Could the Red Sox wind up having to play a Monday doubleheader to complete the 162-game schedule? MLB will surely do everything it can to avoid that, but the league will be watching the weather closely over the next few days.

item.title: [yanksgoyard.com] Yankees' rotation vs. Rays is setting up a potential Wild Card Series mistake
item.dc:creator: Adam Weinrib
item.description: The New York Yankees are almost guaranteed to face the Boston Red Sox in an upcoming best-of-three Wild Card series, and can lock up homefield advantage with either a singular win in their final seven games or one Boston loss. The time is now for forecasting and getting your ducks in a row, and the Yankees have acknowledged as such; resetting Brent Headrick, for example, is more important than going all out to embarrass the Tampa Bay Rays this week. That makes every rotation decision or perceive
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are almost guaranteed to face the Boston Red Sox in an upcoming best-of-three Wild Card series, and can lock up homefield advantage with either a singular win in their final seven games or one Boston loss. The time is now for forecasting and getting your ducks in a row, and the Yankees have acknowledged as such; resetting Brent Headrick, for example, is more important than going all out to embarrass the Tampa Bay Rays this week.
That makes every rotation decision or perceived pattern seem magnified, especially after Boston lined up their starters for their upcoming series with the Cleveland Guardians: Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, Ranger Suárez. Is that the chips falling where they may, or is that foreshadowing? Either way, while winking and nodding, it's probably time to read similarly into the way the Yankees are handlng things.
That's why our eyebrows raised on Sunday when the Yanks revealed that Cam Schlittler and Gerrit Cole will stay on turn in the Rays series (for now), with Schlittler closing the four-game set and Cole pitching Game 3, both staying out of the doubleheader. That will leave Cole with an extra day of rest ahead of the WIld Card opener and Schlittler on normal rest. You're not saying ... ?
All the love in the world to Gerrit Cole, who got closer to securing an all-important Wild Card Series start with his strong appearance in the desert on Friday night. But given that his spot in the rotation in general has been rightly questioned, there is no world where he should start Game 1 over Schlittler. That is not even something that should be rolling around in the canals of my addled gray brain. And yet!
Yankees giving Gerrit Cole the rest he needs ahead of Wild Card Series. Will Cam Schlittler even start vs. Rays?
For now, this is all hypothetical, but ... Cole has always seemed like a candidate for a deciding Game 3, but nothing before it. Would the Yankees really dare to use him in a deciding game with three extra days of rest building up on his right arm?
And, if the Rays clinch the AL East this week and the Yankees lock down their positioning, will they use Schlittler at all in this series? Will he make a perfunctory three-inning cameo just to keep his sea legs ahead of the Sox showdown and prevent overthrowing/overcompensating? The Cy Young race between he and Dylan Cease is informally over, and Cease may not even be healthy enough to make another start. If positioning gets more solidified throughout the week, these decisions only become more fascinating.
As of now, though, before any adjustments ... it seems like there's at least a chance the Yankees are lining up Cole for Game 1 - or working him out of the picture entirely.

item.title: [NBC Sports Boston] Who matters most for Red Sox in playoffs? We ranked the top 10
item.dc:creator: Justin Leger
item.description: The Boston Red Sox have officially clinched a postseason berth, completing one of the most improbable turnarounds in MLB history. But the real test begins next week. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have officially clinched a postseason berth, completing one of the most improbable turnarounds in MLB history.
But the real test begins next week. After falling to the New York Yankees in last year’s Wild Card Series, Boston is looking to make a deeper October run this time around, and it looks like the Yankees will once again stand in the way.
It’s been a total team effort for Boston all season long, but the playoffs are where stars emerge and the margin for error becomes razor thin. While nearly everyone on the postseason roster will play a role, we’ve narrowed it down to the 10 players who could have the biggest impact on how far this team goes.
Here are the 10 most important -- not necessarily the best -- Red Sox players for the 2026 playoffs:
1. Payton Tolle, SP
What a difference a year makes. Last year, Tolle experienced growing pains in his first MLB stint and pitched just 1/3 of an inning in the Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium. This time, he's coming off an exceptional rookie campaign with a chance to start Game 1 in the Bronx.
Tolle will enter the postseason with momentum on his side. The 23-year-old tallied 12 strikeouts while allowing just one run in six innings against Baltimore. He followed that up with six shutout innings against Kansas City, including an immaculate inning to begin the game.
If Tolle continues to perform at this level, he'll give the Red Sox another frontline starter who can match up against other teams' aces. He's the pitcher with the greatest opportunity to change the trajectory of this postseason roster.
If the Red Sox make a deep postseason run, it'll be because their rookie left-hander delivered each time he took the mound on the big stage.
2. Sonny Gray, SP
We're sticking with pitching, because pitching is what propelled this Red Sox club to a postseason berth in the first place.
If Tolle is No. 1, it would be silly not to put Gray right behind him at No. 2. The 36-year-old veteran stabilized the rotation in the wake of Garrett Crochet's injury. He was signed to be the No. 3 starter behind Crochet and Ranger Suarez, but he performed like an ace with a 17-5 record and a 2.82 ERA in 28 starts.
Now, Boston will lean on Gray and his big-game experience to lead the staff in October. Even if he doesn't start Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, Gray will play a huge role in any postseason success.
3. Roman Anthony, LF/DH
The top position player on our list is the 22-year-old many expected to anchor Boston's lineup and produce an MVP-caliber season in 2026. Instead, Anthony spent most of the year on the injured list and has largely struggled in the 50 games he's been healthy. We know what the former No. 1 prospect is capable of, however, and he'll significantly raise the Red Sox' ceiling if he plays up to his potential in the postseason.
The Red Sox will lean heavily on their pitching staff throughout the playoffs, but Anthony is the X-factor in the lineup. This is a completely different club when he gets hot.
All it will take is a signature postseason moment for Red Sox fans to forget about the disappointing start to Anthony's young career.
4. Ranger Suarez, SP
OK, back to pitching. A big reason the Red Sox signed Suarez to a five-year, $130 million contract in free agency is that he has a stellar postseason track record. The 31-year-old boasts a 1.48 ERA across 11 playoff appearances (eight starts) with the Philadelphia Phillies.
The only reason he isn't higher on this list is we project him to be the No. 3 starter, which means we won't even see him if the Sox get swept out of the Wild Card Series. If Boston advances, another strong postseason from Suarez will be critical for their World Series chances.
5. Wilyer Abreu, RF
Abreu is one of Boston's best all-around players, but he's a streaky hitter. The Red Sox' mediocre offense can't afford for him to go cold in the postseason, so he's an incredibly important piece if they hope to make a deep run.
When he's hot, Abreu's bat is elite. He leads the American League with 36 doubles along with 24 homers in 151 games.
As important as his bat will be, Abreu's Gold Glove defense in right field will also be a difference-maker. Postseason games can come down to one defensive miscue, and Abreu has earned a reputation as one of the best defensive right fielders in baseball.
If Abreu can give the Red Sox consistent at-bats and quality defense, he can quietly become one of the most impactful players on the roster over an entire series.
6. Willson Contreras, 1B
We've got the Venezuelan sluggers back-to-back. Contreras has been the Red Sox' most consistent bat all season, and he'll be leaned on heavily in the heart of the lineup throughout the playoffs.
Unlike most of Boston's lineup, Contreras will enter the Wild Card Series with plenty of postseason experience. He won a World Series with the 2016 Chicago Cubs and has 30 playoff games under his belt in total.
With a team-high 27 homers, Contreras will be counted on to supply the Red Sox lineup with power throughout their playoff run. If he goes cold, there will be even more pressure on guys like Anthony, Abreu, and the player who's next up on our list to get runs on the board.
7. Adley Rutschman, C
Rutschman will need to step it up offensively, but his importance goes beyond his bat because of his position. One could argue the role he plays behind the plate is even more crucial.
As Boston's starting catcher, Rutschman will be responsible for managing the pitching staff through almost every postseason game, meaning he'll be involved on almost every pitch thrown. There's also a significant downgrade at catcher if he goes down with an injury, with only Connor Wong and Mickey Gasper as his potential backups.
For the Red Sox to make it far, Rutschman has to be more than just a productive hitter; he must also work seamlessly with the rotation and bullpen while living up to his reputation as one of the best defensive backstops in the league.
8. Aroldis Chapman, CP
Having a closer who can slam the door shut gives clubs a huge advantage come postseason time. The Red Sox are fortunate to have arguably the best of the bunch.
While Chapman wasn't otherworldly in 2026 like he was in 2025, he still was elite with a 1.95 ERA in 52 appearances. He'll look to limit free passes after watching his walk rate jump from 2.2 to 4.1 BB/9 over last year. If he does that, Boston can effectively shorten games by having him available for the ninth inning. He can also single-handedly lose games, automatically making him one of the club's most important players for the postseason.
9. Garrett Whitlock, RP
Boston's bullpen is perhaps its biggest strength heading into the postseason, and that's because of the Whitlock/Chapman combo at the back end. Whitlock has been an elite set-up man with a 1.75 ERA and 0.877 WHIP across 53 appearances this season.
Starters typically have shorter outings in the playoffs, so we could see the Red Sox turn to Whitlock early and often throughout October if they advance past the Wild Card Series. He's the reliever Boston will count on to mow down the heart of an opposing lineup in a high-leverage situation. That could be the difference between a win and a loss, and that's why Whitlock makes the top 10 over some other very important players.
10. Ceddanne Rafaela, CF
Rafaela rounds out our top 10 most important Red Sox players for the postseason, but don't let his ranking fool you. With elite defense in center field and a bat that made a significant leap this season, he can be considered another X-factor for this club in the playoffs.
If Boston makes a deep run, there's a good chance we'll get at least one signature Rafaela moment. The 26-year-old has a knack for coming up big in the clutch, whether it's with a timely extra-base hit or a mind-blowing catch in center field.
Rafaela's glaring absence during his time on the injured list with a quad injury has highlighted his importance to this club. If he's back to full strength in time for the playoffs, that'll give the Red Sox a major boost.
Honorable mentions: 3B Caleb Durbin, SS Trevor Story, LF/DH Jarren Duran, RP Erik Miller, RP Tyron Guerrero, P Brayan Bello and P Jake Bennett.
They didn't crack the top 10, but that doesn't mean they won't have huge roles in October.
Durbin completely changes the outlook of the offense when he's hitting. He's also been an elite defensive third baseman all season long.
Story has been one of Boston's best hitters since returning from the injured list. There's no guarantee that'll carry over into the playoffs, but he'll at least have to be adequate defensively as the team's starting shortstop.
Duran had a 2026 to forget, and with Anthony in left field and Mickey Gasper likely at DH, he'll probably spend a fair amount of time on the bench. Still, he's the type of player who can change a game with one swing, and his speed is a huge factor.
Miller and Guerrero will have major roles at the back end of the bullpen. Bello (if he makes the roster) and Bennett will be leaned on as bulk relievers. Miller has struggled lately, Guerrero is returning from injury, Bello is unproven in the playoffs, and we haven't seen Bennett come out of the 'pen.

item.title: [bostonglobe.com] Red Sox offense has been running on fumes down the stretch - The Boston Globe

item.content:encoded:
Call it a product of injuries or just a slump, but the Red Sox are staggering into the final week of the regular season offensively.
They have averaged 2.82 runs over the last 11 games, hitting .210 with a .621 OPS.
Wilyer Abreu (7 for 36), Mickey Gasper (4 for 25), Jahmai Jones (2 for 18), Isiah Kiner-Falefa (1 for 20), Adley Rutschman (6 for 30), and Nick Sogard (8 for 40) have all gone cold.
Roman Anthony was 5 for 13 with two doubles and a home run over the weekend against the Rays after hitting .137 in his 12 prior games.
The Sox are eighth in the American League in runs scored (678, 4.35 per game). They were third last season at 4.85.
“Just got to stay with it,” interim manager Chad Tracy said after a 5-1 loss against the Rays on Sunday. “Obviously we’ve got to hit and score runs. But we’re getting our way back to health, and we’ll get there.”
The return of two of the team’s top hitters, Willson Contreras and Ceddanne Rafaela, should help.
Contreras has played only four games this month because of a strained left hamstring and a bruised right hand. He started swinging a bat Sunday and hopes to return this week after missing the Rays series.
“It’s getting better every day,” Contreras said Sunday. “We’ll see.”
Contreras leads the team in home runs (27), RBIs (81), and OPS (.905).
Rafaela should be back in the lineup Tuesday after missing 16 games with a right quadriceps strain. He has hit .282 with a .760 OPS, 16 homers, and 70 RBIs.
Caleb Durbin has reached base in 13 consecutive games, raising his on-base percentage from .324 to .338.
Trevor Story has been another positive, hitting .338 with an .869 OPS and 10 RBIs over 19 games since returning from the injured list.
Tests this week
The postseason doesn’t start until Sept. 29, but the Red Sox will get a taste of what’s to come this week at Fenway Park.
They start a three-game series against the Guardians on Tuesday before the Cubs arrive Friday.
The 81-75 Guardians hold a one-game lead over the White Sox in the American League Central. The 87-69 Cubs are tied with the Padres atop the National League wild-card race.
The Guardians have All-Star lefthander Parker Messick (12-9, 2.57) starting Tuesday with Foster Griffin (15-5, 3.67) on Wednesday. Messick faced the Sox in Cleveland on May 30 and allowed one run over five innings.
The Sox have Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez lined up in the series, which could be how they approach the Wild Card Series next week.
Honor for Arias
Shortstop Franklin Arias was named the Eastern League’s Most Valuable Player and Top Prospect by Minor League Baseball. The 20-year-old from Venezuela hit .318 with a .993 OPS in 75 games for Portland before he was promoted to Triple-A Worcester. Sea Dogs first baseman Brooks Bannon also was named to the Eastern All-Star team. The Pitcher of the Year was righthander Anthony Eyanson, who was 4-0 with a 1.69 ERA in 11 games for Portland before going to the Orioles organization in the trade for Rutschman . . . The Sox finished 46-35 on the road, a five-game improvement on last season . . . Assistant general managers Mike Groopman and Taylor Smith interviewed with the Athletics, who are searching for a head of baseball operations after firing David Forst in August. Longtime assistant GM Billy Owens also is a candidate, along with former Nationals GM Mike Rizzo and former Astros GM James Click, who now works for the Blue Jays.
Peter Abraham can be reached at peter.abraham@globe.com. Follow him on Bluesky at peteabeglobe.bsky.social.

item.title: [yanksgoyard.com] Red Sox-Cubs weather nightmare could give Yankees a surprising playoff edge
item.dc:creator: Adam Weinrib

item.content:encoded:
Fans of the Boston Red Sox are about to become bigger fans of the Philadelphia Phillies and San Diego Padres than they've ever been. And fans of the New York Yankees are about to get a renewed interest in destructive weather systems.
With Boston and New York all but fated to meet next week in a best-of-three Wild Card Series, the Yankees are suddenly invested in a chaotic super storm that might interfere with the Sox's meaningful weekend series with the Chicago Cubs. If the Cubs' playoff positioning is at stake - right now, they're tied atop the Wild Card standings with the Padres and one game ahead of the Phillies - these games will need to be completed, whether or not they have any significance to the Sox. Bostonians probably hope the Cubs slip up before they ever arrive at Fenway while the Pads and Phils surge.
It seems very likely these games will need to be completed, though. It also seems very likely these games will be washed out, leading to either a baseball game (or two!) taking up Boston's lone off day before the start of the postseason, or an emergency roadtrip to Chicago disrupting things in a different way.
Will Red Sox insane weather weekend against Cubs hurt their chances against Yankees in playoffs?
Now, counterpoint, we know how much the Red Sox tend to excel when faced with plane trauma or travel trouble of any kind. Does extreme weather also make them superhuman? I, for one, do not want to find out.
Objectively, though, even if they rest all their starters and even if they have zero members of the playoff rotation penciled into this Cubs series, all lined up for the previous showdown with the Cleveland Guardians ... this has to have an effect, doesn't it? It's in MLB's absolute best interest to avoid any nonsense here. Cram a doubleheader into Friday. Tell John Henry he's about to lose some gate receipts and push this whole series to Chicago. The impact on the Wild Card Series is too great.
And you thought this weekend of baseball was meaningless, didn't you, Yankees fans? Joke's on you.
Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suárez will all be out of commission either way, but any undue duress that removes a clean reset point from the Sox while allowing the Yankees to veg out and get in the right mindset can certainly swing things a bit. And if this series is crucial to the Cubs, MLB won't love Boston trying to rest their starters and back away from the competition either. This is about to be fascinating, strange, and a potentially damaging wrinkle in any playoff preview.

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

21 Sep 2026, 22:49 GMT+10

(Photo credit: David Dermer)
The Cleveland Guardians are playing some of their best baseball of the season at the most important time, and they will attempt to extend a five-game winning streak when they visit the Boston Red Sox on Tuesday.
Cleveland (81-75) has a one-game lead over the Chicago White Sox for first place in the American League Central standings with six games remaining. After playing three games at Boston, the Guardians will wrap up the regular season with a three-game road series against the Kansas City Royals.
The Guardians also have a three-game lead over the Texas Rangers, who are at the top of the American League West standings. Cleveland and Texas are among the teams battling for the AL's No. 2 seed, which comes with a first-round bye.
'The feeling in the clubhouse is pretty awesome right now,' Cleveland closer Cade Smith said after he earned his 39th save in 44 opportunities when the Guardians beat the Athletics 1-0 Sunday. 'We've got some momentum. We've got confidence in the way we're playing. We're playing clean baseball.
'There's this kind of calm focus that we're ready to go out there and play. We're looking forward to taking it one game at a time and finishing strong and setting us up for the postseason.'
The Guardians went 10-20 in their first 30 games after the All-Star break and were a season-high five games under .500 (61-66) at that point but have gone 20-9 since then.
'One day at a time,' Cleveland manager Stephen Vogt said. 'We can only control today. Let's go 1-0 every day and let's worry about tomorrow, tomorrow, because here we are, one week to go, six games to go. We're right in it and we have a great opportunity in front of us.'
Despite dropping a 5-1 decision to the Tampa Bay Rays on Sunday, Boston (84-72) clinched a playoff spot when the Houston Astros lost to the Atlanta Braves. A postseason berth didn't seem likely when the Red Sox had a 32-46 record on June 24.
'They didn't take no for an answer,' said interim manager Chad Tracy, who took over a 10-17 team when he replaced Alex Cora on April 26. 'When you work as hard as we have worked, it was almost July (before we got going), and to fight as hard as we did, to put ourselves in the position we did, I don't think you care much how (the spot is clinched). You just want to see your ticket get punched.'
The Red Sox will almost certainly open the playoffs with a best-of-three wild-card series on the road against the New York Yankees. Boston and New York also met in the wild-card round last year, when the Yankees won the series in three games.
Boston also has six regular-season games remaining. After the three-game series against the Guardians, Boston will play three home games against the Chicago Cubs.
Tuesday's pitching matchup features a pair of left-handers in Cleveland's Parker Messick (12-9, 2.57 ERA) and Boston's Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.02). Tolle was originally scheduled to pitch over the weekend against Tampa Bay, but had his start pushed back as Boston lines up its pitching for the postseason.
Messick doesn't have a decision against Boston but has a 4.15 ERA in two career appearances (both starts). Tolle has not pitched against Cleveland during his career.
--Field Level Media

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Clinching celebration solidified need for Red Sox-Payton Tolle contract extension
item.dc:creator: Katie Manganelli

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox's Wild Card clinching ceremony included the usual champagne showers and dripping-wet interviews. Everyone had their moments between the clubhouse party and the team photo, but the expected star of the celebration did not disappont.
Payton Tolle gave Red Sox fans everything they wanted and more out of their playoff-making party. The towering lefty is usually the most hilarious member of the Red Sox, but his antics were turned up to 11 in the presence of more beer than anyone can drink.
Tolle smashed some beers Stone Cold style, danced like no one was watching and gave an under-the-influence interview fans won't soon forget. The best part is that he would probably do many of the same things sober as a judge.
Tolle has grown in to a Red Sox fan favorite in record time. His off-the-field shenanigans match up to the skill he brings on the mound. After his first season-plus with Boston, it should be doing everything in its power to keep Tolle on the team for as long as possible.
Payton Tolle's Wild Card celebration showed just how badly the Red Sox need to extend him
The Red Sox have adopted an early contract extension strategy with many of its young players, including Ceddanne Rafaela, Brayan Bello and Roman Anthony, among others. Alex Speier of The Boston Globe reported on August 18 that Boston hadn't approached Tolle about an extension at the time (subscription required). The Sox have signed so many young players that they could be taking a break, but they should re-start negotiations again for Tolle.
Not only is the 23-year-old an electric personality, he's a force on the mound. The American League's 2026 rookie class is packed to the brim with talent including Kevin McGonigle (the certain winner), Parker Messick and Munetaka Murakami, but Tolle has performed well enough to deserve a mention near the top of this year's list.
Tolle has posted a 3.02 ERA, 1.07 WHIP, 166 strikeouts and 38 walks over 143 innings. The rookie has deepened and sharpened his arsenal this season, his extension (a metric Craig Breslow loves) is elite at a staggering seven-foot-four, his 36.5 percent chase rate sits in the 96th percentile and his 28.9 strikeout percentage ranks near the top of the league. Tolle is an imposing presence on the mound with the prime of his career still years away and the Red Sox should hold onto him for as long as possible.
Tolle will most likely get a start during Boston's Wild Card series, possibly in Game 1. The Red Sox clearly trust him in big moments, he's got personality to share and he's already active in the community — he is the ideal candidate for an early contract extension.

item.title: [heavy.com] Red Sox' Payton Tolle Can Make Franchise History in Postseason

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are set for a pivotal playoff matchup, likely with the New York Yankees in the first round of the postseason.
It’s been a whirlwind of a season for Boston fans after their horrible start under manager Alex Cora and subsequent hot streak under interim manager Chad Tracy. Part of this hot streak has been the emergence of an elite rotation led by rookies and veterans alike.
Their rotation is so good, in fact, that it’s a real discussion of who will start Game 1 and Game 2 between Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suárez. And it’s a good problem to have!
Rob Bradford of WEEI shared that Tolle has a “good shot” at taking the mound in the first game of the series. If he gets the ball in Game 1 or Game 2, he will make franchise history as the youngest pitcher to start the first or second game of a playoff series since Babe Ruth in the 1918 World Series, per former Red Sox director of baseball communications and media relations JP Long.
Should Boston Red Sox Phenom Payton Tolle Start Game 1 or 2?
The Red Sox drafted Tolle in the second round of the 2024 MLB Draft out of Texas Christian University. Teams quickly saw that Tolle had the tools to succeed, as he sprinted through the minors.
He would soon have an elite year in the minors in his first professional season, making it all the way to the majors in 2025. However, it was rough sledding for Tolle as he sported a 6.06 ERA in 16.1 major league innings.
Going into 2o26, he was a top-20 prospect. From the start of the season, he has not disappointed. In 25 starts during 20026 (143 innings), Tolle has a 3.02 ERA with 166 strikeouts and just 38 walks.
He has the second-lowest ERA among qualified starters on the team, just behind Sonny Gray. While you could definitely make an argument that the veteran Gray should start Game 1, Tolle has been a monster against the Yankees this season.
In his season debut on April 23, Tolle went six innings, allowing just three hits, one walk, one run and striking out 11 batters. On June 26, he would face New York again, going seven innings and allowing just one hit and two walks with seven strikeouts.
Gray has the regular-season production, postseason experience and fuel, being a former Yankees castoff. However, Tolle seems to be at his best when playing against New York and other AL East teams.
Either way, Tolle will likely be making history not seen since the Great Bambino in over a century.
What About Game 3 and Moving Forward?
Suárez should be locked in for a top-3 start, if necessary. In 27 starts, Suárez has a 3.27 ERA in 143.1 innings with 135 strikeouts. The two-time All-Star is also a formidable playoff pitcher, with a minuscule 1.48 ERA in 11 postseason games.
After him, it gets a bit murkier. While you don’t need a full five-man rotation in the playoffs, it’s likely necessary to have a fourth dependable starter.
Rookie Jake Bennett was cruising through his first dozen career starts. However, in his last seven starts, he has a 5.40 ERA. He may be unlikely to shoulder such a burden in his first postseason. It also complicates things that 2025 Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet has been out since late April and will likely be a bullpen arm if and when he returns in 2026.
And perhaps the most shocking positive development has been the improvement of Brayan Bello. In his first 10 games, Bello was a disaster. In his last 15, he has been borderline elite with a 2.98 ERA. This was highlighted by an eight-inning performance on Saturday. If needed, Bello could likely be a starter or bulk reliever in the playoffs.
Whatever the case may be, the Boston Red Sox could be a dangerous team in October, with their monster pitching staff at the head of it all.

item.content:encoded:
Now, they have six regular-season games left to prepare for what is to come.
One big objective will be to get postseason baseball back to Fenway Park for the first time since 2021. After losing in three games in the 2025 AL Wild Card Series to the Yankees at Yankee Stadium, the ending felt too abrupt.
It has already been an improbable turnaround for the Red Sox, surging from 14 games under .500 on June 25 and getting to the postseason. There is a belief within the clubhouse that more magic can happen.
“I think we can make a run,” said rookie lefty Payton Tolle. “I think we’ve got the guys. I think we can get hot. We’re just going to continue to play the way that we play. That team baseball we’ve been playing. You play to get to the postseason and to give yourself a shot to go to the World Series.”
Without further ado, here are some key talking points heading into the playoffs.
What could the postseason roster look like?
C: Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
1B: Willson Contreras
2B: Nick Sogard
SS: Trevor Story
3B: Caleb Durbin
UTIL: Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Mickey Gasper
OF: Jarren Duran, Ceddanne Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Braiden Ward
DH: Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
SP: Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle
Bullpen: Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, Erik Miller, Greg Weissert, Brayan Bello, Jake Bennett, Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck
The most intriguing decision for the position-player roster surrounds whether to add Ward, who set the Triple-A Worcester record with 61 stolen bases this season, as a pinch-running specialist. Dave Roberts, anyone?
The bullpen situation also bears watching. Considering that Crochet hasn’t pitched since April 25 and Houck’s next appearance will be his first in the Majors since 2025, the club will monitor how both rehabbers are throwing before finalizing the roster. This could influence if the club carries Bennett as a reliever. Jovani Morán is another option from the left side.
When does the postseason begin?
For the Red Sox, the fun starts on Sept. 29, when interim manager Chad Tracy’s club participates in an AL Wild Card Series, with all games in the best-of-three series to be played on the road. The Yankees, unless they improbably take the AL East from the Rays, will be the Red Sox opponent in what will be yet another chapter in the richest rivalry in baseball. The only other scenario that can stave off another rivalry match would be the Red Sox slipping to the No. 6 seed. They lead the current No. 6 seed, the White Sox, by four games.
How have the Red Sox performed against the Yankees this season?
Last year, Boston’s hopes of getting a playoff game at Fenway Park for the first time since ‘21 ended when the team lost Game 3 of the Wild Card Series to … the Yankees in the Bronx. So, yes, this would be a rematch between the rivals. In a form befitting the rivalry, the regular-season series swayed back and forth, with New York ultimately taking seven of the 13 head-to-head encounters.
The Yankees swept the Red Sox at Fenway from April 21-23 in what wound up being Alex Cora’s last home series managing Boston. Fast forward to the Bronx from June 5-7, and the sides split, with the middle game getting postponed due to rain. For the Red Sox, their entire season started to turn around with a four-game sweep at Fenway from June 25-28. And for the Yankees, home field for this potential series was essentially wrapped up when they took three out of four from the Sox at the end of August to clinch the season series.
Will Aaron Judge be active for the Wild Card Series?
Judge’s potential participation in the series will be a huge focal point. The Yankees’ captain, limited to 66 games this season, was recently placed on the injured list again with a right calf strain. Though the Yankees have played more games without Judge than with him, his absence could make a difference for Boston.
What happens in the unlikely scenario the Red Sox slip from the No. 5 seed to the No. 6 spot?
In that case, the Red Sox would play the division champion with the worst record, which at this point would be whoever emerges victorious in a shaky AL West.
Which health situations should be monitored as the regular season winds down?
Where to start? There are many to choose from.
Contreras suffered a badly bruised knuckle between his right ring finger and pinkie when he was hit by a pitch on Sept. 17. He admitted he will be out for “days,” but hopes to be back before the postseason. It was a good sign that Contreras was able to grip a bat and take some swings on Sunday.
All eyes will be on Crochet to see if it’s possible to activate him for the playoffs as a reliever even though he hasn’t pitched since April 25 due to left shoulder inflammation.
Rafaela, the Red Sox's All-Star center fielder, has been out since Sept. 3 with a right quadriceps strain but should return before the regular season ends.
How does the rotation line up for the Red Sox?
If not for the near season-long loss of Crochet to this point, the Game 1 starter wouldn’t be in question. Tracy reordered his rotation for the upcoming series, going with Tolle on Tuesday against the Guardians, followed by Gray on Wednesday and Suarez on Thursday. Could this be the same order the Sox open the playoffs with? Tracy isn’t ready to reveal those plans yet.
How much postseason experience does Boston’s projected roster have?
Contreras and Chapman both won World Series rings while playing for the 2016 Cubs. Chapman added another one with the Rangers in ‘23. Kiner-Falefa was with Toronto last season, meaning he got to play in the epic Dodgers-Blue Jays World Series, losing one of the most dramatic Game 7s ever.
Rutschman played in five postseason games during his time with the Orioles, but none beyond the Division Series. Several players in Boston’s young core got their first taste of postseason experience last year in Abreu, Rafaela and Duran. Durbin went to the NLCS with the Brewers in ‘25. Houck and Whitlock are the only players remaining on the Boston team that came two wins from making the World Series in ‘21. Veteran shortstop Story had a solid Wild Card Series in the Bronx last year.
Suarez (4-1, 1.48 ERA in 11 outings, eight starts) had his share of October moments in Philadelphia, and Gray has a 3.26 ERA in six career playoff starts.

item.content:encoded:
It’s not remotely the right time to start talking about offseason movement, but there is movement afoot. Two of Craig Breslow’s assistant GMs, Mike Groopman and Taylor Smith, have already conducted preliminary interviews for the big chair in Sacramento after the A’s fired Dave Forst back in August. (Sean McAdam, MassLive)
Here in Boston, though, we’re unlikely to see a search for a new boss in a while. Craig Breslow earned himself quite a bit of rope this season, thanks to a decisive move that paid off big time in firing Alex Cora. “I believed in the players that we had, and I felt it was really important that we acted definitively and decisively when we did, so that we could create an environment around the players that was supportive, that would allow them to thrive, and they responded,” he said. “And, while there may have been some people that questioned what this group was capable of, I think they answered.” (Peter Abraham, Boston Globe)
And here’ s a look at some of the key moments of the season that got this team where it is today. Remember the ninth inning comeback against the Mets that came after that long-delayed flight? How about Caleb Durbin’s home run off Cam Schlittler? (Tim Healey, Boston Globe)
But, strangely enough, when it came time to clinch the playoffs, it wasn’t a Red Sox player who did the dirty work, though it was a Red Sox legacy player. “And the man with the game-winning three-run homer that would, in the end, send both the Braves and the Red Sox to the postseason? Well, baseball is quite sentimental, and it also has a sense of humor, so, obviously, it was Mike Yastrzemski.“ (Shanthi Sepe-Chepuru, MLB.com)
But the fact that the Sox clinched on a loss didn’t dampen the celebration. “There was a lot of beer!” said Payton Tolle. “It was a slobberknocker.” (Rob Bradford, WEEI)
But before the slobberknocker could get slobbin’, Chad Tracy addressed his team to sum up the season that was. “I want to express gratitude for everyone in the room,” he said. “I’m so grateful for you guys, for our staff, for everybody. You stared impossible in the face. The position we were in, you beat it back and said, ‘The hell with that, we’re going to the playoffs.’ And you did.” (Jen McCaffrey, The Athletic)
So the Sox are in the dance. But for how long? That’s anyone’s guess, but Red Sox fans are apparently more optimistic than the fans of any other American league team. (Stephen J. Nesbitt, The Athletic)

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Payton Tolle Can Make Red Sox Playoff History 108 Years After Babe Ruth
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown
